**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾. The definite form of *al-hamd* (praise) together with the *lam* of exclusivity (*lam al-ikhtisas*) indicates that all instances of praise belong exclusively to Allah, glory be to Him, as its verification was already discussed in the opening of the Book (*Fatihah al-Kitab*). The relative clause (*al-mawsul*) is in the genitive position as an adjective (*na't*) or an apposition (*badal*), or in the accusative by way of exclusivity, or in the nominative by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). The meaning of ﴿to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is that everything in them is in His dominion and under His control; He does with it what He wills and judges concerning it as He desires. Every blessing that reaches the servant is among what He created for him and bestowed upon him. So His being praised for what is in the heavens and the earth is praise for the blessings He has bestowed upon His creatures from what He created for them.

Since He had explained that worldly praise from His servants who praise Him belongs exclusively to Him, He then explained that otherworldly praise likewise belongs exclusively to Him. He said: ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾. His saying *lahu* ("to Him") is connected either to the praise itself, or to what is connected to the predicate of the praise, namely *fi al-akhirah* ("in the Hereafter"). The latter is connected to a general implied verb such as "is established" or the like. The meaning is that, to Him exclusively, belongs the praise of His servants who praise Him in the abode of the Hereafter when they enter Paradise, as in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]; His saying: ﴿"Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this"﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]; His saying: ﴿"Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief"﴾ [Fatir: 34]; His saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty" [Fatir: 35]; and His saying: ﴿And their last call will be, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. So He, glory be to Him, is the one praised in the Hereafter just as He is the one praised in this world, and He is the owner of the Hereafter just as He is the owner of this world. ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, who perfected the affairs of both abodes, ﴿the All-Aware﴾ of the affairs of His creatures in them. It has been said that the difference between the two kinds of praise is that praise in this world is an act of worship, while praise in the Hereafter is delight and joy, because obligation (*taklif*) has ended there.

Then, glory be to Him, mentioned some of what His knowledge encompasses of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, i.e., what goes into it of rain, treasure, or buried things; ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, of crops, plants, and living creatures; ﴿and what descends from the heaven﴾, of rains, snow, hail, thunderbolts, and blessings, and among that is what descends from it of His angels and His scriptures to His prophets; ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, of angels and the deeds of the servants.

The majority of readers read *yanzilu* with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a light *zay* (*takhfif*), attributing it to *ma* ("what"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Sulami read it with a *dammah* on the *ya'* and a *tashdid* on the *zay*, attributing it to Allah, glory be to Him. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful﴾ to His servants, ﴿the Most Forgiving﴾ of their sins.

﴿And those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come to us."﴾ The intended referents of these speakers are disbelievers in general, or specifically the disbelievers of Mecca. The meaning of "The Hour will not come to us" is that it will not come in any state, denying its existence, not merely denying its coming at the time of their speaking or during their lifetime while accepting that it will exist later. So Allah refuted them and commanded His Messenger to say to them: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you."﴾ This oath is for emphasizing the certainty of its coming. The majority read *latatiyannakum* with the feminine (*fawqiyyah*) form, referring to *al-sa'ah* (the Hour). Talq al-Mu'allim read it with the masculine (*tahtiyyah*) form, interpreting *al-sa'ah* as "the Day" or "the time."

Talq said: "I heard our teachers reading it with the *ya'*," meaning the masculine form, according to the sense, as if He had said: "The Resurrection or its command will surely come to you," just as He said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come?﴾ [al-Nahl: 33].

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *'alimu al-ghayb* ("Knower of the unseen") with *raf'* (nominative), as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is ﴿does not escape Him﴾, or by assuming an implied subject. 'Asim, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read it with *jarr* (genitive), as an adjective of *Rabbi* ("my Lord"). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *'allam* with *jarr*, in the intensive form (*sigha al-mubalagah*).

The meaning of ﴿does not escape Him﴾ is that it is not hidden from Him, nor concealed from Him, nor distant from Him: ﴿not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth escapes Him, nor what is smaller than that﴾ (the atom's weight), ﴿nor greater﴾ than it, ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*).

The meaning is: except that it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet, which contains the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him. So this emphasizes the negation of escaping.

The majority read *ya'zubu* with a *dammah* on the *zay*. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a *kasrah*. Al-Farra' said: "The *kasrah* is more beloved to me, and both are dialects. It is said: *'azaba ya'zubu* with a *dammah*, and *ya'zibu* with a *kasrah*, when it means to be far away and to be absent."

The majority read *wa-la asghara wa-la akbara* ("nor smaller nor greater") with *raf'* (nominative), as beginning (*ibtida'*), with the predicate being "except in a clear Book," or by coordination with *mithqal* (atom's weight). Qatadah and al-A'mash read them with *nasb* (accusative), coordinating them with *dharrah* (atom), or by taking *la* to be the *la* of absolute negation (*la al-tabri'ah*), whose noun is built on *fath*.

The *lam* in ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is for causation (*ta'lil*), connected to His saying "it will surely come to you." That is, the purpose of the Hour's coming is to reward believers with reward and disbelievers with punishment. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers back to the relative clause, meaning: those who believed and did righteous deeds. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾ of their sins, ﴿and a noble provision﴾, which is Paradise, because of their faith and their righteous deeds, together with Allah's bounty upon them, glory be to Him.

Then He mentioned the group of disbelievers who will be punished at the coming of the Hour, saying: ﴿And those who strove against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them﴾, i.e., they strove to nullify Our verses revealed to the messengers, discredited them, and prevented people from them. The meaning of *mu'ajizin* ("seeking to frustrate") is competing, thinking that they could escape Us and not be overtaken, because they believed that they would not be resurrected. It is said: *'ajazahu* and *a'jazahu*, when one overcomes and outstrips another.

The majority read *mu'ajizin*. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Mujahid, and Abu 'Amr read *mu'ajjizin*, meaning discouraging people from belief in the verses. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those who strove, ﴿for them is a punishment of painful torment﴾. *Rijz* is punishment, so *min* is for explanation (*lil-bayan*). It has been said that *rijz* is the worst and most severe punishment, but the first view is preferable. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59]. The majority read *alim* ("painful") with *jarr*, as an adjective of *rijz*. Ibn Kathir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with *raf'*, as an adjective of *'adhab*. *Alim* means intensely painful.

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. When He mentioned those who strove to nullify the verses of Allah, He mentioned those who believe in them. The meaning of ﴿those who have been given knowledge see﴾ is that they know, and they are the Companions.

Muqatil said: "They are the believers among the People of the Book." It has also been said that they are all the Muslims. The relative clause is the first object (*maf'ul awwal*) of *yara* ("see"), and the second object is *al-haqq* ("the truth"). The pronoun is a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*).

The majority read *al-haqqa* with *nasb*. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with *raf'*, as the predicate of the pronoun, and the clause is in the accusative position as the second object. This is the dialect of Tamim, who recognize what comes after the separating pronoun. Al-Farra' claimed that the preferred reading is *raf'*, but others disagreed and said that *nasb* is more common.

It has been said that His saying *yara* is coordinated with *liyajziya* ("that He may reward"), and this was the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. It was objected to that *liyajziya* is connected to *latatiyannakum*, and one does not say: "The Hour will come to you so that those who have been given knowledge may see that the Qur'an is true." The better view is that this is a new independent statement, to refute what those who strove against the verses say. That is, their saying indicates their ignorance, since they oppose what the people of knowledge know about the Qur'an. ﴿And it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ is coordinated with *al-haqq*, a verb coordinated with a noun, because it is in the sense of a noun, as in His saying: ﴿Ranks, and those who grip﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "and gripping," as if it were said: "and guiding." It has also been said that it is an independent statement whose subject is a pronoun referring to the subject of *unzila* ("was revealed"), which is the Qur'an. *Sirat* means path, so the meaning is: it guides to the path of the Mighty in His dominion, the Praiseworthy in His creation. The intended meaning is that it guides to the religion of Allah, which is monotheism.

Then, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of speech of those who deny the resurrection, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, i.e., some of them said to others: ﴿"Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you"﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., "Shall we guide you to a man who will tell you of a strange matter and a wondrous report, which is that ﴿when you are torn into complete pieces﴾, i.e., you are scattered in every way, cut into every kind of fragment, and after your death you become dust and crumbled bones, ﴿you will be in a new creation"﴾, i.e., you will be created anew, resurrected from your graves alive, and return to the forms you were in. This statement was said by some of them to others in mockery of what Allah promised through His Messenger concerning resurrection. They framed the speech as jest, laughing at what he says about it.

*Idha* ("when") is in the accusative position with the verb *muzziqtum* ("you are torn").

Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible for the governing verb to be *yunabbi'ukum* ("will inform you"), because he does not inform them at that time. Nor is it permissible for the governing word to be what comes after *inna* ("indeed"), because it does not govern what precedes it."

Al-Zajjaj permitted that the governing word be an omitted verb, the meaning being: "When you are torn into complete pieces, you will be resurrected," or "you will be informed that you will be resurrected when you are torn." Al-Mahdawi said: "*Muzziqtum* cannot govern it, because it is a genitive complement (*mudaf ilayhi*), and the complement cannot govern the element it is attached to."

The root of *mazq* is tearing things apart. It is said: *thawbun mazid* ("a torn garment"), *mumazzaq*, *mutamazziq*, and *mamzuq*.

Then, glory be to Him, related of these disbelievers that they doubted what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) promised them of resurrection, between two possibilities. They said: ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾, i.e., is he lying in what he says, or is there insanity in him such that he does not understand what he says? The *hamzah* in *aftara* ("has he invented") is the interrogative *hamzah*, and the connecting *hamzah* was dropped because of it, as was discussed before in His saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ [Maryam: 78].

Then, glory be to Him, refuted what they said about His Messenger, saying: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error﴾, i.e., the matter is not as they claim. Rather, they are those who went astray from understanding and from grasping the realities. They disbelieved in the Hereafter and did not believe in what he brought them. Because of that, they will be in lasting punishment in the Hereafter, and in this world they are in deep error, far from the truth.

Then He rebuked them, glory be to Him, for their audacity in denial, clarifying to them that this came from them only because of their failure to reflect and contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth, and that whoever is able to create this immense creation is not unable to resurrect from His creatures what is less than that and return them to what they were, in essence and attributes.

The meaning of ﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾ is that when they look, they see the sky behind them and in front of them, and likewise when they look at the earth, they see it behind them and in front of them. So the heavens and the earth encompass them. He is therefore able to send down upon them whatever punishment He wills because of their disbelief, their denial of His Messenger, and their rejection of resurrection.

This verse includes two matters. The first is that the creation which Allah created from the heaven and the earth indicates complete power over what is less than it, namely resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81].

The second matter: a warning to them that the One who created the heavens and the earth in this form, which encompasses all the creatures in them, is able to hasten punishment upon them. ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ as it swallowed Qarun, ﴿or We shall make pieces of the sky fall upon them﴾, i.e., fragments, ﴿from the sky﴾ as He made it fall upon the people of al-Aykah. So how can they feel safe from that?

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿in nasha'﴾ with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), and likewise ﴿nakhsif﴾ and ﴿nusqit﴾.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the ya' (third person) in the three verbs, i.e., "in yasha' Allah" ("if God wills").

Al-Kisa'i alone read with idgham (assimilation) of the fa' into the ba' in "nakhsif bihim" (nakhsif bihim). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "That is not permissible, because the fa' is produced from the inner part of the lower lip and the tips of the upper incisors, unlike the ba'."

The majority read "kisafan" with the sukun on the sin, while Hafs and al-Sulami read it with a fatha on it.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the creation of the heavens and the earth mentioned, ﴿is a clear sign and an evident proof for every servant who turns back (muníb)﴾, i.e., returns to his Lord in repentance and sincerity. He specified the one who turns back because he is the one who benefits from reflection.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, he said: "From rain," ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, he said: "From plants," ﴿and what descends from the sky﴾, he said: "From the angels," ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, he said: "The angels."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿of a painful punishment (rijz alim)﴾, he said: "Al-rijz is the painful, agonizing punishment." And regarding His words ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾, he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding the verse, he said: "It means the believers among the People of the Book."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Shall we direct you to a man"﴾, he said: "The polytheists of Quraysh said that," ﴿"when you are torn to shreds, every shredding"﴾, meaning: "when the earth has consumed you and you have become dust and bones, and the beasts and birds have torn you apart," ﴿"indeed you will be in a new creation"﴾, meaning: "indeed you will be made alive and resurrected." They said this in denial of it. ﴿"Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?"﴾ He said: "They said either he lies against God, or he is insane." ﴿"Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the sky and the earth?"﴾ They said: "If you look to your right and to your left, and in front of you and behind you, you will see the sky and the earth." ﴿"If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them"﴾ as We swallowed those before them, ﴿"or We shall make pieces of the sky fall upon them"﴾, i.e., fragments from the sky. If He wills to punish them through His sky, He does so; and if He wills to punish them through His earth, He does so; and all His creation is an army for Him. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns back﴾, he said: "a penitent who turns in devotion to God."

**Tafsir of Surah Saba'**

It is a Meccan surah. Al-Qurtubi said: "According to all scholars, except one verse about which they disagreed, which is His saying: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6]. One group said it is Meccan, and another group said it is Madinan. The disagreement concerning the meaning of this verse and about whom it was revealed will come later, if Allah wills." Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surah Saba' was revealed in Mecca."

The better view is that this is a new independent statement, to refute what those who strove against the verses say. That is, their saying indicates their ignorance, since they oppose what the people of knowledge know about the Qur'an. ﴿And it guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ is coordinated with *al-haqq*, a verb coordinated with a noun, because it is in the sense of a noun, as in His saying: ﴿Ranks, and those who grip﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "and gripping," as if it were said: "and guiding." It has also been said that it is an independent statement whose subject is a pronoun referring to the subject of *unzila* ("was revealed"), which is the Qur'an. *Sirat* means path, so the meaning is: it guides to the path of the Mighty in His dominion, the Praiseworthy in His creation. The intended meaning is that it guides to the religion of Allah, which is monotheism.

Then, glory be to Him, mentioned another kind of speech of those who deny the resurrection, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, i.e., some of them said to others: ﴿"Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you"﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., "Shall we guide you to a man who will tell you of a strange matter and a wondrous report, which is that ﴿when you are torn into complete pieces﴾, i.e., you are scattered in every way, cut into every kind of fragment, and after your death you become dust and crumbled bones, ﴿you will be in a new creation"﴾, i.e., you will be created anew, resurrected from your graves alive, and return to the forms you were in. This statement was said by some of them to others in mockery of what Allah promised through His Messenger concerning resurrection. They framed the speech as jest, laughing at what he says about it.

*Idha* ("when") is in the accusative position with the verb *muzziqtum* ("you are torn").

Al-Nahhas said: "It is not permissible for the governing verb to be *yunabbi'ukum* ("will inform you"), because he does not inform them at that time. Nor is it permissible for the governing word to be what comes after *inna* ("indeed"), because it does not govern what precedes it."

Al-Zajjaj permitted that the governing word be an omitted verb, the meaning being: "When you are torn into complete pieces, you will be resurrected," or "you will be informed that you will be resurrected when you are torn." Al-Mahdawi said: "*Muzziqtum* cannot govern it, because it is a genitive complement (*mudaf ilayhi*), and the complement cannot govern the element it is attached to."

The root of *mazq* is tearing things apart. It is said: *thawbun mazid* ("a torn garment"), *mumazzaq*, *mutamazziq*, and *mamzuq*.

Then, glory be to Him, related of these disbelievers that they doubted what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) promised them of resurrection, between two possibilities. They said: ﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾, i.e., is he lying in what he says, or is there insanity in him such that he does not understand what he says? The *hamzah* in *aftara* ("has he invented") is the interrogative *hamzah*, and the connecting *hamzah* was dropped because of it, as was discussed before in His saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen?﴾ [Maryam: 78].

Then, glory be to Him, refuted what they said about His Messenger, saying: ﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far error﴾, i.e., the matter is not as they claim. Rather, they are those who went astray from understanding and from grasping the realities. They disbelieved in the Hereafter and did not believe in what he brought them. Because of that, they will be in lasting punishment in the Hereafter, and in this world they are in deep error, far from the truth.

Then He rebuked them, glory be to Him, for their audacity in denial, clarifying to them that this came from them only because of their failure to reflect and contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth, and that whoever is able to create this immense creation is not unable to resurrect from His creatures what is less than that and return them to what they were, in essence and attributes.

The meaning of ﴿what is before them and what is behind them﴾ is that when they look, they see the sky behind them and in front of them, and likewise when they look at the earth, they see it behind them and in front of them. So the heavens and the earth encompass them. He is therefore able to send down upon them whatever punishment He wills because of their disbelief, their denial of His Messenger, and their rejection of resurrection.

This verse includes two matters. The first is that the creation which Allah created from the heaven and the earth indicates complete power over what is less than it, namely resurrection, as in His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81].

The second matter: a warning to them that the One who created the heavens and the earth in this form, which encompasses all the creatures in them, is able to hasten punishment upon them. ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them﴾ as it swallowed Qarun, ﴿or We shall make pieces of the sky fall upon them﴾, i.e., fragments, ﴿from the sky﴾ as He made it fall upon the people of al-Aykah. So how can they feel safe from that?

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿in nasha'﴾ with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), and likewise ﴿nakhsif﴾ and ﴿nusqit﴾.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the ya' (third person) in the three verbs, i.e., "in yasha' Allah" ("if God wills").

Al-Kisa'i alone read with idgham (assimilation) of the fa' into the ba' in "nakhsif bihim" (nakhsif bihim). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "That is not permissible, because the fa' is produced from the inner part of the lower lip and the tips of the upper incisors, unlike the ba'."

The majority read "kisafan" with the sukun on the sin, while Hafs and al-Sulami read it with a fatha on it.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the creation of the heavens and the earth mentioned, ﴿is a clear sign and an evident proof for every servant who turns back (muníb)﴾, i.e., returns to his Lord in repentance and sincerity. He specified the one who turns back because he is the one who benefits from reflection.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, he said: "From rain," ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, he said: "From plants," ﴿and what descends from the sky﴾, he said: "From the angels," ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, he said: "The angels."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿of a painful punishment (rijz alim)﴾, he said: "Al-rijz is the painful, agonizing punishment." And regarding His words ﴿and those who have been given knowledge see﴾, he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding the verse, he said: "It means the believers among the People of the Book."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Shall we direct you to a man"﴾, he said: "The polytheists of Quraysh said that," ﴿"when you are torn to shreds, every shredding"﴾, meaning: "when the earth has consumed you and you have become dust and bones, and the beasts and birds have torn you apart," ﴿"indeed you will be in a new creation"﴾, meaning: "indeed you will be made alive and resurrected." They said this in denial of it. ﴿"Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?"﴾ He said: "They said either he lies against God, or he is insane." ﴿"Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the sky and the earth?"﴾ They said: "If you look to your right and to your left, and in front of you and behind you, you will see the sky and the earth." ﴿"If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them"﴾ as We swallowed those before them, ﴿"or We shall make pieces of the sky fall upon them"﴾, i.e., fragments from the sky. If He wills to punish them through His sky, He does so; and if He wills to punish them through His earth, He does so; and all His creation is an army for Him. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for every servant who turns back﴾, he said: "a penitent who turns in devotion to God."

**Tafsir of Surah Saba'**

It is a Meccan surah. Al-Qurtubi said: "According to all scholars, except one verse about which they disagreed, which is His saying: ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ [Saba': 6]. One group said it is Meccan, and another group said it is Madinan. The disagreement concerning the meaning of this verse and about whom it was revealed will come later, if Allah wills." Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surah Saba' was revealed in Mecca."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

His saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾. The definite form of *al-hamd* (praise) together with the *lam* of exclusivity (*lam al-ikhtisas*) indicates that all instances of praise belong exclusively to Allah, glory be to Him, as its verification was already discussed in the opening of the Book (*Fatihah al-Kitab*). The relative clause (*al-mawsul*) is in the genitive position as an adjective (*na't*) or an apposition (*badal*), or in the accusative by way of exclusivity, or in the nominative by assuming an implied subject (*mubtada'*). The meaning of ﴿to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is that everything in them is in His dominion and under His control; He does with it what He wills and judges concerning it as He desires. Every blessing that reaches the servant is among what He created for him and bestowed upon him. So His being praised for what is in the heavens and the earth is praise for the blessings He has bestowed upon His creatures from what He created for them.

Since He had explained that worldly praise from His servants who praise Him belongs exclusively to Him, He then explained that otherworldly praise likewise belongs exclusively to Him. He said: ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾. His saying *lahu* ("to Him") is connected either to the praise itself, or to what is connected to the predicate of the praise, namely *fi al-akhirah* ("in the Hereafter"). The latter is connected to a general implied verb such as "is established" or the like. The meaning is that, to Him exclusively, belongs the praise of His servants who praise Him in the abode of the Hereafter when they enter Paradise, as in His saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us"﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]; His saying: ﴿"Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this"﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]; His saying: ﴿"Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief"﴾ [Fatir: 34]; His saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty" [Fatir: 35]; and His saying: ﴿And their last call will be, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. So He, glory be to Him, is the one praised in the Hereafter just as He is the one praised in this world, and He is the owner of the Hereafter just as He is the owner of this world. ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, who perfected the affairs of both abodes, ﴿the All-Aware﴾ of the affairs of His creatures in them. It has been said that the difference between the two kinds of praise is that praise in this world is an act of worship, while praise in the Hereafter is delight and joy, because obligation (*taklif*) has ended there.

Then, glory be to Him, mentioned some of what His knowledge encompasses of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, i.e., what goes into it of rain, treasure, or buried things; ﴿and what comes out of it﴾, of crops, plants, and living creatures; ﴿and what descends from the heaven﴾, of rains, snow, hail, thunderbolts, and blessings, and among that is what descends from it of His angels and His scriptures to His prophets; ﴿and what ascends into it﴾, of angels and the deeds of the servants.

The majority of readers read *yanzilu* with a *fath* on the *ya'* and a light *zay* (*takhfif*), attributing it to *ma* ("what"). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Sulami read it with a *dammah* on the *ya'* and a *tashdid* on the *zay*, attributing it to Allah, glory be to Him. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful﴾ to His servants, ﴿the Most Forgiving﴾ of their sins.

﴿And those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come to us."﴾ The intended referents of these speakers are disbelievers in general, or specifically the disbelievers of Mecca. The meaning of "The Hour will not come to us" is that it will not come in any state, denying its existence, not merely denying its coming at the time of their speaking or during their lifetime while accepting that it will exist later. So Allah refuted them and commanded His Messenger to say to them: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come to you."﴾ This oath is for emphasizing the certainty of its coming. The majority read *latatiyannakum* with the feminine (*fawqiyyah*) form, referring to *al-sa'ah* (the Hour). Talq al-Mu'allim read it with the masculine (*tahtiyyah*) form, interpreting *al-sa'ah* as "the Day" or "the time."

Talq said: "I heard our teachers reading it with the *ya'*," meaning the masculine form, according to the sense, as if He had said: "The Resurrection or its command will surely come to you," just as He said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that the command of your Lord should come?﴾ [al-Nahl: 33].

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *'alimu al-ghayb* ("Knower of the unseen") with *raf'* (nominative), as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is ﴿does not escape Him﴾, or by assuming an implied subject. 'Asim, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read it with *jarr* (genitive), as an adjective of *Rabbi* ("my Lord"). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *'allam* with *jarr*, in the intensive form (*sigha al-mubalagah*).

The meaning of ﴿does not escape Him﴾ is that it is not hidden from Him, nor concealed from Him, nor distant from Him: ﴿not an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth escapes Him, nor what is smaller than that﴾ (the atom's weight), ﴿nor greater﴾ than it, ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*).

The meaning is: except that it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet, which contains the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him. So this emphasizes the negation of escaping.

The majority read *ya'zubu* with a *dammah* on the *zay*. Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a *kasrah*. Al-Farra' said: "The *kasrah* is more beloved to me, and both are dialects. It is said: *'azaba ya'zubu* with a *dammah*, and *ya'zibu* with a *kasrah*, when it means to be far away and to be absent."

The majority read *wa-la asghara wa-la akbara* ("nor smaller nor greater") with *raf'* (nominative), as beginning (*ibtida'*), with the predicate being "except in a clear Book," or by coordination with *mithqal* (atom's weight). Qatadah and al-A'mash read them with *nasb* (accusative), coordinating them with *dharrah* (atom), or by taking *la* to be the *la* of absolute negation (*la al-tabri'ah*), whose noun is built on *fath*.

The *lam* in ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is for causation (*ta'lil*), connected to His saying "it will surely come to you." That is, the purpose of the Hour's coming is to reward believers with reward and disbelievers with punishment. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers back to the relative clause, meaning: those who believed and did righteous deeds. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾ of their sins, ﴿and a noble provision﴾, which is Paradise, because of their faith and their righteous deeds, together with Allah's bounty upon them, glory be to Him.

Then He mentioned the group of disbelievers who will be punished at the coming of the Hour, saying: ﴿And those who strove against Our verses, seeking to frustrate them﴾, i.e., they strove to nullify Our verses revealed to the messengers, discredited them, and prevented people from them. The meaning of *mu'ajizin* ("seeking to frustrate") is competing, thinking that they could escape Us and not be overtaken, because they believed that they would not be resurrected. It is said: *'ajazahu* and *a'jazahu*, when one overcomes and outstrips another.

The majority read *mu'ajizin*. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Mujahid, and Abu 'Amr read *mu'ajjizin*, meaning discouraging people from belief in the verses. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those who strove, ﴿for them is a punishment of painful torment﴾. *Rijz* is punishment, so *min* is for explanation (*lil-bayan*). It has been said that *rijz* is the worst and most severe punishment, but the first view is preferable. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59]. The majority read *alim* ("painful") with *jarr*, as an adjective of *rijz*. Ibn Kathir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read it with *raf'*, as an adjective of *'adhab*. *Alim* means intensely painful.

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. When He mentioned those who strove to nullify the verses of Allah, He mentioned those who believe in them. The meaning of ﴿those who have been given knowledge see﴾ is that they know, and they are the Companions.

Muqatil said: "They are the believers among the People of the Book." It has also been said that they are all the Muslims. The relative clause is the first object (*maf'ul awwal*) of *yara* ("see"), and the second object is *al-haqq* ("the truth"). The pronoun is a separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*).

The majority read *al-haqqa* with *nasb*. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with *raf'*, as the predicate of the pronoun, and the clause is in the accusative position as the second object. This is the dialect of Tamim, who recognize what comes after the separating pronoun. Al-Farra' claimed that the preferred reading is *raf'*, but others disagreed and said that *nasb* is more common.

Then He (Glory be to Him) mentioned among His servants who turn back to Him (*munībīn*), Dawud and Sulayman, as He said regarding Dawud: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. And He said regarding Sulayman: ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body, then he turned back in repentance﴾ [Sad: 34]. Then He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Dawud a bounty from Us﴾. That is, We gave him, because of his turning back (to Us), a bounty from Us above the rest of the prophets.

Scholars differed about this bounty in several views. It was said: prophethood. It was said: the Psalms (*al-Zabur*). It was said: knowledge. It was said: strength, as in His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the one of might﴾ [Sad: 17]. It was said: the subjugation of the mountains, as in His words: ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾. It was said: repentance. It was said: judging with justice, as in His words: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾ [Sad: 26]. It was said: the softening of iron, as in His words: ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾. It was said: a beautiful voice. The preferred view is that the bounty mentioned is what Allah mentions after it, from His words ﴿O mountains﴾ to the end of the verse. The phrase ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾ is implicitly governed by "saying" (*al-qawl*): that is, We said, "O mountains!" The word *ta'wib* means glorification (*tasbih*), as in His words: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him﴾ [Sad: 18].

Abu Maysarah said: it means glorification in the language of Abyssinia (Habasha).

Whenever Dawud glorified (Allah), the mountains glorified along with him. The meaning of the mountains' glorification is that Allah makes them capable of it, or He creates glorification in them as a miracle for Dawud. It was also said: the meaning of *awwibi* is "travel with him," from *ta'wib*, which is traveling the whole day, and from it is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

We caught up with a tribe who had traveled through the day,
after we had pushed back the rays of the sun while the horse's flank was winged.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿awwibi﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the waw, in the imperative form, from *ta'wib*, which means repeating the chant, or glorifying, or traveling, or wailing.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read *ūbī* with a damma on the hamza, as an imperative from *āba yaʾūbu*, meaning "to return," that is: return with him.

The majority read ﴿and the birds﴾ in the accusative (*nasb*), coordinated with *faḍlan* (the object of "gave") with the meaning: "And We subjected the birds to him," because giving him them is subjecting them to him. Or it is coordinated with the place (*maḥall*) of *yā jibālu*, since it is accusative in meaning, as the sense is: "We called the mountains and the birds."

Sibawayh and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said that its accusative case is by a hidden verb, with the meaning: "And We subjected the birds to him."

Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said it may be an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ah*), as you say: "The water and the plank became level."

Al-Kisa'i said it is coordinated with *faḍlan*, but with an omitted genitive construction (*taqdir muḍāf maḥdhūf*), meaning: "We gave him a bounty and the glorification of the birds."

Al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Abu Nawfal, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Hurmuz, and Maslamah ibn 'Abd al-Malik read it in the nominative (*raf'*), coordinated with the wording of "the mountains," or with the pronoun in *awwibi*, due to the separation between the coordinated and what it is coordinated with.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾ is coordinated with "We gave him," meaning: We made it soft, so that he could work with it as he wished.

Al-Hasan said: the iron became like wax; he worked it without fire.

Al-Suddi said: the iron in his hand was like wet clay, dough, or wax; he shaped it however he wished, without fire and without striking with a hammer. Muqatil said likewise, and he would finish making a coat of mail in part of a day.

﴿That make full coats of mail﴾: regarding *an* here there are two possibilities. The first is that it is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyyah*) with the preposition deleted, meaning: "with [the command] make..." The second is that it is the explanatory *an* (*mufassirah*) for His words "And We made iron soft." But this view is questionable, because the explanatory *an* occurs only after a saying or something having the meaning of saying. Some scholars supposed a verb in it with the meaning of saying, saying the estimate is: "And We commanded him: make..."

His words "full" (*sābighāt*) are an adjective of a deleted noun, meaning: full coats of mail. The "full" ones are the complete, wide ones. It is said: "The coat of mail or the garment or other things 'sabagha' (was complete)" when it covers all that is on it and has some excess remaining.

﴿And be moderate in the weaving﴾: *al-sard* is the weaving of coats of mail. It is said *al-sard* and *al-zard*, as *al-sarrad* and *al-zarrad* are said for the maker of coats of mail. *Al-sard* also means stitching; it is said "*sarada yasrudu*" when he stitched, and from it "*sarada al-kalam*" when he delivered speech in a continuous flow. From the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not speak continuously as you do."

Sibawayh said: from it comes *sarīd*, meaning "running smoothly." The meaning of weaving coats of mail is making them firm, and that the arrangement of their rings be consistent and not varied. From it is the verse of Labid:

He wove coats of mail, doubling their weaving,
so that he might attain long life, not to be cheated.

And the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Upon them both are two woven coats, which Dawud finished,
or which the makers of full coats of mail, the Tubba', made.

Qatadah said: coats of mail before Dawud were heavy, so he was commanded to measure in that which combines lightness and protection. That is: measure what you take from these two meanings in its proper proportion, so you do not aim for protection so that it becomes heavy, nor for lightness so that it removes defense. Ibn Zayd said: the measure he was commanded with concerns the size of the ring: that is, do not make them small so that they are weak and the coat cannot defend, and do not make them large so that they are heavy on the one who wears them.

It was said: the measure concerns the rivet: that is, do not make the rivet of the coat thin so that it is loose, nor thick so that it breaks the rings.

Then He addressed Dawud and his family, saying: ﴿And work righteousness﴾, that is, righteous deeds, as in His words: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba': 13]. Then He gave the reason for the command to righteous deeds in His words: ﴿Indeed I am Seeing of what you do﴾, that is, nothing of that is hidden from Me.

﴿And to Sulayman, the wind﴾: the majority read *al-rīḥa* in the accusative, with the estimate: "And We subjected the wind to Sulayman," as al-Zajjaj said. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him, read it in the nominative, as a subject and predicate: "And for Sulayman, the wind is firm or subjected." The majority read *al-rīḥ*; al-Hasan, Abu Hayah, and Khalid ibn Ilyas read *al-riyāḥ* in the plural.

﴿Its morning course is a month, and its evening course is a month﴾: that is, it traveled in the morning the distance of a month, and in the evening likewise. The sentence is either a new sentence explaining the subjugation of the wind, or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The meaning is that it traveled in one day the distance of two months.

Al-Hasan said: he would set out from Damascus and take a midday rest at Istakhr, and between them is a month's journey for a fast traveler; then he would leave Istakhr and spend the night at Kabul, and between them is a month's journey.

﴿And We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him﴾. *Al-qiṭr* is melted copper.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: a spring of brass flowed for him for three days and their nights, like the flow of water. People today only work with what was given to Sulayman. The meaning is: We caused the spring of copper to flow for him just as We made iron soft for Dawud. Qatadah said: Allah caused a spring to flow for him which he used for whatever he wished.

﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him by the permission of his Lord﴾: *man* is the subject, and *ya'malu* is its predicate. *Min al-jinn* is connected to it or to a deleted element, as a circumstantial clause. Or *man ya'malu* is coordinated with *al-rīḥ*, and *min al-jinn* is a circumstantial clause. The meaning: We subjected to him those who worked before him, being from the jinn, by the permission of their Lord, that is, by His command.

*Al-idhn* is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) attributed to its agent, and the prepositional phrase is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is: subjected or made easy by the command of their Lord.

﴿And whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾, that is: whoever of the jinn turns away from Our command which We commanded him with, namely obedience to Sulayman, ﴿We will make him taste of the punishment of the Blaze﴾. Most exegetes said this is in the Hereafter; it was also said it is in this world.

Al-Suddi said: Allah assigned to the jinn an angel with a whip of fire in his hand, and whoever deviated from the command of Sulayman, he would strike him with that whip, a blow that would burn him.

Then He (Glory be to Him) mentioned what the jinn did for Sulayman, saying: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed﴾. The "min" in His words ﴿of sanctuaries (*min maḥārīb*)﴾ is explanatory. *Al-maḥārīb* in the language means every elevated place, and they are the lofty buildings and high palaces.

Al-Mubarrad said: the *miḥrab* is only what is reached by stairs, and from this it is said that the place where one prays is a *miḥrab*, because it is raised and honored.

Mujahid said: the *maḥārīb* are below the palaces.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the *miḥrab* is the most noble part of a house, and from it is the verse of the poet:

What harm is it to him if I mention companions
like gazelles of the sand in the sanctuaries of Aqyal?

Al-Dahhak said: the *maḥārīb* here means mosques. *Al-tamāthīl* is the plural of *timthāl*, which is everything you have made similar to something, that is, you formed it in its likeness, of copper, glass, marble, or otherwise.

It was said: these statues were images of prophets, angels, scholars, and righteous people, and they would make them in the mosques so that people would see them and increase in worship and striving.

It was said: they were statues of things that are not animals.

This verse has been used as evidence that depiction was permissible in the law of Sulayman, and that this was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the law of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

*Al-jifān* is the plural of *jafnah*, which is a large bowl.

*Al-jawāb* is the plural of *jābiyah*, which is a basin like a pool. It was also said: it is a large pool that gathers water, that is, collects it.

Al-Wahidi said: the exegetes said: meaning bowls as large as the watering troughs of camels, so that a thousand men could gather around one bowl and eat from it.

Al-Nahhas said: it is better to keep the *yā'* in *al-jawābī*. Whoever deletes the *yā'* says the rule is that *al-* (the definite article) enters upon an indefinite noun without changing it from its state; since it is said *jawābin* and the *alif-lam* entered, it was kept in its state and the *yā'* was deleted.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is said "*jabawtu al-māʾ*" and "*jabaytuhu*" in the basin, meaning I collected it; *al-jābiyah* is the basin in which water is collected for camels.

Al-Nahhas said: *al-jābiyah* is a great cooking pot and a large, great basin in which something is collected, that is, gathered; from it: "I collected the tax (*kharāj*)" and "I collected the locusts," meaning I gathered them in a cloak.

﴿And cooking pots fixed in place﴾: Qatadah said: they are copper cooking pots that were in Persia. Al-Dahhak said: they are cooking pots carved out of solid mountains, which the devils made for him. The meaning of *rāsiyāt* is firm, not moved or carried because of their great size.

Then He (Glory be to Him) commanded them to righteous deeds in general, that is, Sulayman and his family, saying: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾. That is: and We said to them, "Work by obeying Allah, O family of Dawud, in gratitude to Him for what He has given you," or "Work a work of gratitude," being an attribute of a deleted verbal noun, or "they worked for gratitude" as an object of purpose, or as a circumstantial clause, meaning "thankful," or as an object. Obedience was called gratitude because it is among its kinds. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun with a deleted verb of its kind, meaning: "Be thankful, with thanks."

Then, after commanding them to thank Him, He explained that those among His servants who are thankful are not many, saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾, that is: those who work by My obedience and are thankful for My blessing are few. *Qalīl* is raised as a predicate that precedes its subject. *Min ʿibādiya* is an attribute of it. *Al-shakūr* is the subject.

﴿So when We decreed death upon him﴾, that is: We judged death upon him and obligated it on him. ﴿Nothing indicated to them his death except a creature of the earth﴾, meaning the termite (*al-arada*).

It is read *al-ara̱ḍi* with a fatha on the *rāʾ*, that is, the eating. It is said: "*aradat al-khashabah aradan*" when the termite ate the wood.

The meaning of ﴿it devoured his staff﴾ is: it ate his staff upon which he was leaning. *Al-minsaʾah* is the staff in the language of Abyssinia, or it is derived from "*nasaʾtu al-ghanam*," meaning I drove the sheep.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-minsaʾah* is that with which one is driven, that is, chased away.

The majority read *minsaʾatahu* with a fatha on the hamza. Ibn Dhakwan read it with a silent hamza. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with a pure *alif*.

Al-Mubarrad said: some Arabs change its hamza to an *alif*, and he recited:

When you walk upon the staff from old age,
the play and the flirtation have distanced themselves from you.

Like the majority's reading is the verse of the poet:

We struck his face with a staff,
so he became humiliated and debased by that.

And like it:

Was it because of a rope that you struck your father, not you,
with a staff, while your rope has pulled your own ropes?

And what indicates Ibn Dhakwan's reading is the verse of Tarafah:

Strong like the planks of the Aran, I have driven them
over a clear path, as if it were the back of a sword-strip.

﴿فَلَمّا خَرَّ﴾ means "when he fell," that is, collapsed. ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ﴾ means "it became clear to the jinn," that is, it became manifest to them. It is from *tabayyantu al-shay'* (I knew the thing), meaning "the jinn came to know." ﴿أنْ لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الغَيْبَ ما لَبِثُوا في العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ means: if what they claim, that they know the unseen, were true, they would have known of his death and would not have remained for a long time after his death in the humiliating torment, the labor he had ordered them to perform and their obedience to him, while he was already dead.

Muqatil said: "The humiliating torment" is hardship and toil in work. Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes (*al-mufassirun*) said: In the time of Sulayman, people used to say that the jinn know the unseen. When Sulayman remained standing, leaning on his staff, dead for a year, while the jinn kept doing those heavy tasks they used to do during Sulayman's lifetime, they did not perceive his death until the termite (*al-arada*) ate his staff, and he fell dead. Then they knew of his death, and the people knew that the jinn do not know the unseen.

It is also possible that ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ﴾ is from *tabayyana al-shay'* (the thing became clear), not from *tabayyantu al-shay'*, meaning it became apparent and manifest. Then *an* (that) and what follows it is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion, a grammatical construction in which the substituted phrase is related to the original by containment) for *al-jinn*, with an implied omitted element. The meaning would be: the matter of the jinn became clear to people, namely that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating torment. Or: it became clear that the jinn, had they known the unseen, etc.

The majority (*al-jumhur*) read ﴿تَبَيَّنَتِ﴾ in the active voice, with *al-jinnu* as its subject.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ya'qub read *tubuyyinat* in the passive voice. The meaning of both readings is known from what we have already mentioned.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿أوِّبِي مَعَهُ﴾, that he said: "Glorify (Him) along with him." Similar was narrated from Abu Maysarah, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿وألَنّا لَهُ الحَدِيدَ﴾, that he said: "Like dough."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from him as well, regarding His words ﴿وقَدِّرْ في السَّرْدِ﴾, that he said: "The rings of iron."

'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Hakim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿وقَدِّرْ في السَّرْدِ﴾, that he said: "Do not hammer the nails so that the rings become too wide and loose, and do not make the nails too thick and the rings too narrow so that they break. Make it measured."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd bin Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through several chains from him as well, regarding His words ﴿وأسَلْنا لَهُ عَيْنَ القِطْرِ﴾, that he said: "The *qitr* is *al-nuhas*" (copper).

Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: "*Al-qitr* is copper, which no one was able to work after Sulayman. People after him only worked with what had been given to Sulayman."

'Abd bin Humayd narrated from Mujahid, who said: "*Al-qitr* is yellow copper (*al-sufr*)."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿وتَماثِيلَ﴾, that he said: "Sulayman made statues of copper and said: 'O Lord, breathe spirit into them, for they are stronger for service.' So Allah breathed spirit into them, and they served him. Isfindiyar was among their remnants." Then it was said to David and Sulayman: ﴿اعْمَلُوا آلَ داوُدَ شُكْرًا وقَلِيلٌ مِن عِبادِيَ الشَّكُورُ﴾ ("Work, family of David, in gratitude; and few of My servants are grateful").

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿كالجَوابِ﴾, that he said: "Like the basins (*al-jawbah*) of the earth." And ﴿وقُدُورٍ راسِياتٍ﴾ ("and cooking pots set firm"), he said: "Its tripods are part of it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His words ﴿وقَلِيلٌ مِن عِبادِيَ الشَّكُورُ﴾, that he said: "It means: few of My servants are those who affirm My oneness (*al-muwahhidin*) with their monotheism."

These same narrators also narrated from him: "Sulayman remained leaning on his staff for a year after he died. Then he fell at the end of the year. The jinn took a staff like his and a beast like his, and they let it graze on it, and it ate it within a year." Ibn 'Abbas used to read: ﴿فَلَمّا خَرَّ تَبَيَّنَتِ الجِنُّ﴾ to the end of the verse. Sufyan said: "In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: *wa-hum yad'abuna lahu hawlan*" ("while they toiled for him for a year").

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When Sulayman prayed, he would see a tree growing before him, and he would say to it, 'What is your name?' It would say, 'So-and-so.' He would say, 'For what purpose are you?' It would say, 'For such-and-such.' If it was for planting, it was planted, and if it was for medicine, it was written down. One day he prayed, and there was a tree growing before him. He said to it, 'What is your name?' It said, 'Al-kharrub' (the carob). He said, 'For what purpose are you?' It said, 'For the ruin of this house.' Sulayman said: 'O Allah, conceal my death from the jinn, until mankind knows that the jinn do not know the unseen.' Then he prepared a staff and leaned on it, and Allah took his soul while he was leaning on it. He remained dead for a year while the jinn kept working. Then the termite ate it, and it fell. At that moment they knew of his death." So it became clear to mankind (*al-ins*) that the jinn, ﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ الغَيْبَ ما لَبِثُوا في العَذابِ المُهِينِ﴾ ("had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating torment"). Ibn 'Abbas used to read it that way. The jinn were thankful to the termite, so wherever it was, they brought it water.

Al-Hakim narrated it and authenticated it, from Ibn 'Abbas, as a statement of a Companion (*mawquf*). Al-Daylami narrated from Zayd bin Arqam, as a statement traced to the Prophet (*marfu'*), that he said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'I have favored My servants with three things. I placed the beast (*al-dabbah*) upon the grain, and were it not so, kings would hoard it as they hoard gold and silver. I placed the stench upon the body, and were it not so, no beloved would bury his beloved. And I removed sorrow, and were it not so, offspring would perish.'"

(p-1193)

Then He (Glory be to Him) mentioned among His servants who turn back to Him (*munībīn*), Dawud and Sulayman, as He said regarding Dawud: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. And He said regarding Sulayman: ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body, then he turned back in repentance﴾ [Sad: 34]. Then He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Dawud a bounty from Us﴾. That is, We gave him, because of his turning back (to Us), a bounty from Us above the rest of the prophets.

Scholars differed about this bounty in several views. It was said: prophethood. It was said: the Psalms (*al-Zabur*). It was said: knowledge. It was said: strength, as in His words: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the one of might﴾ [Sad: 17]. It was said: the subjugation of the mountains, as in His words: ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾. It was said: repentance. It was said: judging with justice, as in His words: ﴿O Dawud, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people with truth﴾ [Sad: 26]. It was said: the softening of iron, as in His words: ﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾. It was said: a beautiful voice. The preferred view is that the bounty mentioned is what Allah mentions after it, from His words ﴿O mountains﴾ to the end of the verse. The phrase ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾ is implicitly governed by "saying" (*al-qawl*): that is, We said, "O mountains!" The word *ta'wib* means glorification (*tasbih*), as in His words: ﴿Indeed We subjected the mountains to glorify with him﴾ [Sad: 18].

Abu Maysarah said: it means glorification in the language of Abyssinia (Habasha).

Whenever Dawud glorified (Allah), the mountains glorified along with him. The meaning of the mountains' glorification is that Allah makes them capable of it, or He creates glorification in them as a miracle for Dawud. It was also said: the meaning of *awwibi* is "travel with him," from *ta'wib*, which is traveling the whole day, and from it is the verse of Ibn Muqbil:

We caught up with a tribe who had traveled through the day,
after we had pushed back the rays of the sun while the horse's flank was winged.

The majority read ﴿and the birds﴾ in the accusative (*nasb*), coordinated with *faḍlan* (the object of "gave") with the meaning: "And We subjected the birds to him," because giving him them is subjecting them to him. Or it is coordinated with the place (*maḥall*) of *yā jibālu*, since it is accusative in meaning, as the sense is: "We called the mountains and the birds."

Sibawayh and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said that its accusative case is by a hidden verb, with the meaning: "And We subjected the birds to him."

Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas said it may be an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ah*), as you say: "The water and the plank became level."

Al-Kisa'i said it is coordinated with *faḍlan*, but with an omitted genitive construction (*taqdir muḍāf maḥdhūf*), meaning: "We gave him a bounty and the glorification of the birds."

Al-Sulami, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Abu Nawfal, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Hurmuz, and Maslamah ibn 'Abd al-Malik read it in the nominative (*raf'*), coordinated with the wording of "the mountains," or with the pronoun in *awwibi*, due to the separation between the coordinated and what it is coordinated with.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾ is coordinated with "We gave him," meaning: We made it soft, so that he could work with it as he wished.

Al-Hasan said: the iron became like wax; he worked it without fire.

Al-Suddi said: the iron in his hand was like wet clay, dough, or wax; he shaped it however he wished, without fire and without striking with a hammer. Muqatil said likewise, and he would finish making a coat of mail in part of a day.

﴿That make full coats of mail﴾: regarding *an* here there are two possibilities. The first is that it is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyyah*) with the preposition deleted, meaning: "with [the command] make..." The second is that it is the explanatory *an* (*mufassirah*) for His words "And We made iron soft." But this view is questionable, because the explanatory *an* occurs only after a saying or something having the meaning of saying. Some scholars supposed a verb in it with the meaning of saying, saying the estimate is: "And We commanded him: make..."
