Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *li-Saba'* without tanwin, as a diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*), by interpreting it as a tribe. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The first reading is supported by His saying *fi masakinihim* (in their dwelling places). Had it been understood as a tribe, it would have said *fi masakinihā* (in its dwelling places). The first reading is attested in the verse of the poet:

> The arrivals, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
> the buffalo hides have bitten their necks.

Also attested for the second reading is the verse of the poet:

> Of Saba', the present ones, Ma'rib, when
> they build, apart from its channel, the dam.

Qunbul, Abu Haywah and al-Jahdari read *li-Saba'* with a sukun on the hamzah, and it has also been read with the hamzah changed into an alif.

The majority read *fi masakinihim* in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, and the reason for preferring it is that they had many dwellings and numerous homes. Hamzah and Hafs read it in the singular with a fathah on the kaf.

Al-Kisa'i read it in the singular with a kasrah on the kaf. This reading was also read by Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash. The justification for the singular is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that covers the few and the many, or it is a noun of place used with the sense of the plural. These dwellings that they had are the ones now called Ma'rib, and between it and Sana'a is a journey of three nights. The meaning of His saying *ayah* (a sign) is a proof, a clear indication of the perfection of Allah's power and the wonder of His craftsmanship. Then He explained this sign, saying: ﴿two gardens, on the right and on the left﴾. Their raising (*irtfa'uhuma*) is either as an apposition (*badal*) of *ayah*, as al-Farra' said, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Zajjaj said, or as the subject whose predicate is ﴿on the right and on the left﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this last view, but it has the problem that it is not permissible to begin with an indefinite noun without a justification (*musawwigh*).

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *jannatayn* in the accusative, treating it as a second predicate, with *ayah* as its subject. These two gardens were on the right and the left of their valley and surrounded it from both of its sides. Their dwellings were in the valley, and the sign was the two gardens. A woman would walk between them with a basket on her head, and it would fill with all kinds of fruit that fell down without her touching it with her hand.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the sign that was for the people of Sheba in their dwellings was that they did not see in them a gnat, a fly, a flea, a louse, a scorpion, a snake, or any other vermin. When a caravan came to them with lice in their clothes, the lice died upon seeing their houses.

Al-Qushayri said: He did not mean two gardens only, but that on both sides, to the right and the left, on each side there were many orchards. ﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord﴾: that is, it was said to them, and there was no command in the strict sense, but the intended meaning is that they were enabled to enjoy those blessings. It is also said that the angels said this to them. The provision is the fruits of the two gardens. It is also said that they were addressed this way through their prophet, and [the verse means]: and give thanks to Him for what He has provided you of these blessings, and act in obedience to Him and avoid His disobedience. The clause ﴿a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ is a new sentence (*mustanfa'ah*) explaining the reason that requires gratitude.

The meaning: this is a good land because of the abundance of its trees and the goodness of its fruits. It is also said that the meaning of its being good is that it is not salt-marshy (*sabkhah*). It is also said that there are no vermin in it. Mujahid said: it is Sana'a. The meaning of ﴿and a forgiving Lord﴾ is that the Bestower of blessings upon them is a forgiving Lord for their sins. Muqatil said: the meaning is, "and your Lord, if you give thanks for what He provided you in it, is a forgiving Lord of sins." It is also said that He combined for them the goodness of the land and forgiveness only to indicate that provision may contain something unlawful.

Warsh read *baldatun* and *rabbun* in the accusative, as a form of praise, or by supposing "dwell in a land and give thanks to a Lord."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they did after this blessing with which He had favored them. So He said: ﴿but they turned away﴾ from giving thanks, and ﴿disbelieved in Allah and denied their messengers﴾. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to the people of Sheba thirteen prophets, and they denied them. Wahb said the same.

Then, when they turned away from giving thanks for the blessing, Allah sent upon them a punishment by which He stripped them of what He had bestowed upon them. So He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim﴾. This was because the water used to come to the land of Sheba from the valleys of Yemen. They built a dam (*radm*) between two mountains and held the water back, and in that dam they made three gates, one above another. They used to irrigate from the upper gate, then the second, then the third, and so they became fertile and their wealth increased. When they denied their messengers, Allah sent a rat which gnawed through that dam until it broke, and the water entered their gardens and drowned them, and the flood buried their houses. This is the flood of al-Arim. *Al-'Arim* is the plural of *'arimah*, which is the dam that holds back the water. Qatadah and others said the same.

Al-Suddi said: *al-'Arim* is a name for the dam. The meaning is: We sent upon them the flood of the dam, the 'Arim. 'Ata' said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the valley.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the rat that breached the dam for them, which is called *al-Khuld*. The flood was attributed to it because it was the cause of its flow. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-'Arim* is one of the names of the mouse. Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih said: *al-'Arim* is red water which Allah sent into the dam, and it split and destroyed it. It is also said that *al-'Arim* is the name of heavy rain, and it is also said that it is the name of a violent flood. The root meaning of *al-'irامah* is strength, harshness and difficulty. One says: *'arama* so-and-so, when he became severe and difficult.

It is reported from Ibn al-A'rabi that he said: *al-'Arim* is the flood that cannot be withstood.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-'Arim* is everything that is a barrier between two things.

﴿And We exchanged for them their two gardens for two gardens﴾: that is, We destroyed their two gardens which contained those good fruits and fine varieties, and We gave them in their place two gardens with nothing good in them, and no benefit for them from what grew in them. For this reason He said: ﴿of bitter produce (*dhawatay ukulin khamt*)﴾. The majority read *ukulin* with tanwin and without its being annexed to *khamt*. Abu 'Amr read it with annexation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-khamt* is the tamarisk (*arak*), and many of the exegetes said the same.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-khamt* is every bitter tree with thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: every plant in which there is bitterness that cannot be eaten.

Al-Mubarrad said: everything that changed into something not desired is called *khamt*, and from this comes milk when it has turned. The reading of the majority is preferable to that of Abu 'Amr.

*Khamt* is an attribute of *ukul* or an apposition to it, because *ukul* is itself the *khamt*.

Al-Akhfash said: the annexation is better in Arabic usage, like "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*) and "a house of brick" (*dar ajurr*). The better interpretation of *khamt* is what al-Khalil and those with him mentioned.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-khamt* is a kind of tamarisk that has a edible fruit. Calling the substitute "two gardens" is by way of matching (*mushakalah*) or mockery of them. *Al-athl* is the well-known tree resembling the tamarisk (*tarfa'*), so said al-Farra' and others. He said: except that it is taller than the tamarisk. Its singular is *athalah* and its plural *athalat*.

Al-Hasan said: *al-athl* is wood. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the *nutar* tree. The first view is preferable, and the *athl* has no fruit.

*Al-sidr* is a well-known tree. Al-Farra' said: it is the *samur*. Al-Azhari said: there are two kinds of *sidr* tree: a wild one from which no benefit is taken and which is not suitable for washing, and which has a bitter fruit that is not eaten, and this is what is called *al-dall*. The second is the *sidr* that grows on water, whose fruit is the *nabq* (jujube), and whose leaf is a washing agent, resembling the *'unnab* tree.

It has been said: He described the *sidr* as "few" because among it there is a kind whose fruit is good to eat, and this is the second kind mentioned by al-Azhari.

Qatadah said: while their trees were among the best trees, Allah changed them into the worst of trees because of their deeds, so He destroyed their fruit-bearing trees and grew in their place *arak*, tamarisk, and *sidr*.

It is possible that His saying *qalil* (few) refers to all that was mentioned: the *khamt*, the *athl* and the *sidr*.

The indication in His saying *dhalika* (that) refers to what has preceded of the exchange, or to the verbal noun of *jazaynahum*. The *ba'* in *bima kafaru* is causal: that is, that exchange, or that recompense, is because of their disbelief in the blessing by turning away from giving thanks for it. ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾: that is, Do We requite this recompense, by stripping the blessing and sending down the punishment, except the one who is extremely ungrateful and excessive in it?

The majority read *yujazi* with a *ya'* vowelled with a *dammah* and the *za'* with a *fathah*, in the passive voice. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with *nun* and a *kasrah* on the *za'*, in the active voice, with Allah as the agent, glory be to Him. The word *al-kafur* is in the nominative under the first reading and in the accusative under the second. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the second reading, and said: because before it is *jazaynahum* (We requited them). The apparent meaning of the verse is that He requites none but the ungrateful, though the people of disobedience are also requited. Some people said the meaning of the verse is: He does not inflict this recompense, which is uprooting and destruction, except upon one who has disbelieved.

Mujahid said: the believer has his sins expiated, while the disbeliever is requited for every deed he did.

Tawus said: it is the scrutiny of the reckoning, but the believer is not scrutinized.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that He requites the disbeliever with an equal recompense, one like for like. Al-Nahhas preferred this answer.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed a number of visible towns﴾. This is coordinated with His saying ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾: that is, and it was part of their story that We placed between them and the towns We had blessed with water and trees. These towns are the towns of the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿Towns visible (qura zahirah)﴾: that is, continuous, one after another. Their trade route ran from their land, which is Ma'rib, to al-Sham. They would spend the night in one town and take their midday rest in another until they returned, and they had no need to carry provisions from their land to al-Sham. So this is part of the narrative of what Allah bestowed upon them.

Al-Hasan said: these towns were between Yemen and al-Sham. It was said that they numbered 4,700 towns. It was also said they were between Medina and al-Sham.

Al-Mubarrad said: the "visible towns" are well known, and they were called visible because of their visibility: when you leave one, the next one appears to you, so they were visible towns, that is, well known. One says: this is a visible matter, meaning a known matter.

﴿And We determined within them the journeying (al-sayr)﴾: that is, We made the journey from one town to another a single fixed measure, and that was half a day, as the exegetes said. Al-Farra' said: that is, We placed between each two towns half a day's journey, so that the midday rest would be in one town and the night in another, until one reached al-Sham. A person exerts himself in travel only for lack of provisions, water, and fear of the road. When provisions and security are available, he does not burden himself with hardship, but stops wherever he wishes.

The summary: Allah, glory be to Him, enumerated the blessings for them, then mentioned the calamities that befell them, then returned to enumerate the remaining blessings He had bestowed on them, which lie outside their land, namely the connection of towns between them and the places to which they wished to travel. Then after that He mentioned their being exchanged for deserts and wastelands, as will come. His saying ﴿Travel therein﴾ is on the assumption of a saying: that is, and We said to them, "Travel in those connected towns." It is a command of enablement: that is, and We enabled them to travel in them whenever they wished. ﴿Nights and days, secure﴾ from what they feared. The accusative of *layali* and *ayyaman* is adverbial of time (*zarfiyyah*), and the accusative of *aminin* is a circumstantial (*hal*).

Qatadah said: they used to travel without fear, nor hungry nor thirsty. They used to travel a distance of four months in security; no one would harm another, and even if a man met the killer of his father, he would not touch him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that they did not give thanks for the blessing but sought hardship and toil: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart."﴾ This utterance from them was out of insolence and transgression, since they grew weary of the blessing and did not endure well-being. So they wished for long journeys and for distance between their homelands, and they asked God, exalted is He, to place between them and the Levant, in place of those closely connected villages abundant in water, trees, and security, deserts, wastelands, and open plains with widely separated regions. God granted them their request, destroyed those closely connected villages, and took away the good, the water, and the trees that were in them. Their supplication was thus like the supplication of the Children of Israel, when they said: ﴿Then call upon your Lord for us that He bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 61), in place of the manna and the quails, and like the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and so on.

The majority of readers recited *Rabbana* with a fatha (*naṣb*), as a vocative construction (*munada mudaf*, a vocative noun followed by a genitive construction, i.e., "O our Lord"), and they also recited *bā'id* (as an imperative). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited *ba'id* with a shadda on the ʿayn (*bayyid*, intensive form). Ibn al-Sumayfa recited it with a ḍamma on the ʿayn as a past-tense verb (*buʿida*), so the meaning of this reading is complaint about the distance of the journeys. Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu al-ʿĀliya, Nasr ibn ʿĀsim, and Yaʿqub recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma (as the subject) and *baʿada* (with a fatha on the ʿayn) as a past-tense verb, in the construction of *mubtada'* and *khabar* (subject and predicate), meaning: "Our Lord has put far apart the distances of our journeys." This reading is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it, saying: "They only asked for something closer than that nearness which existed between them and the Levant through the closely connected villages, out of insolence, arrogance, and ingratitude for the blessing."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma and *baʿʿada* with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda, so the meaning of this reading is complaint that their Lord had made the distances between their journeys far apart, although they were close and connected by villages, trees, and water; this would then be part of their insolence. The brother of al-Hasan al-Basri recited, like the earlier reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa, but with *bayna* in the nominative as the subject (*fāʿil*), as is said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bond has been severed﴾ (al-Anʿam: 94). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj transmitted a reading similar to this one, but with *bayna* in the accusative as an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), with the estimate: "Our journey has become far, between our journeys."

Al-Nahhas said: When these readings differ in meaning, it is not permissible to say that one of them is better than the other, just as one does not say that about isolated reports (*akhbar al-ahad*) when their meanings differ. Rather, He informed about them that they asked their Lord to make the distance between their journeys far, and when He did that to them, they complained and were harmed. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, by disbelieving in God, being insolent toward His blessing, and exposing themselves to His punishment. ﴿So We made them narrations﴾, so that people speak of their news.

The meaning is: We made them people of stories that those after them would tell, in wonder at their deed and taking lesson from their condition and their end. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾, i.e., We scattered them in every direction through the lands, completely scattering them. This clause explains "made them narrations." When God, glorified is He, drowned their place and took away their garden, they dispersed throughout the lands, and the Arabs came to use them as proverbs, saying: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'" (*tafarraqū ayādī Sabā'*).

Al-Sha'bi said: So the Ansar joined Yathrib, Ghassan went to the Levant, the Azd went to ʿUmān, and Khuza'a went to Tihama.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story and what God did to them, are clear signs and manifest indications ﴿for every steadfast, grateful one﴾, i.e., for everyone who is greatly patient and grateful. He specified *ṣabbār shakūr* (steadfast and grateful) because they are the ones who benefit from admonitions and signs.

﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾. The majority recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress and *Iblīsu* in the nominative and *ẓannahu* in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), i.e., he confirmed about them an assumption that he assumed, or he was right in his assumption, or it is in the adverbial sense (*ẓarf*). The meaning is that he assumed about them that if he led them astray they would follow him, and he found them to be so. It may also be in the accusative as the object (*mafʿūl*), or with the removal of the preposition.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and ʿĀṣim recited *ṣaddaqa* with a shadda and *ẓannahu* in the accusative as its object. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: That is, he confirmed the assumption that he assumed. Mujahid said: He assumed an assumption and confirmed his assumption, so it was as he assumed. Abu Ja'far, Abu al-Jahja', al-Zuhri, and Zayd ibn ʿAli recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress, *Iblīsa* in the accusative, and *ẓannuhu* in the nominative. Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for this reading in my view, though al-Farra' permitted it, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it, making *al-ẓann* the subject of *ṣadaqa* and *Iblīs* its object. The meaning is that Iblis's assumption had embellished something for him regarding them, and his assumption was confirmed, as if he said: "And indeed the assumption of Iblis was confirmed concerning them." It was narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he recited both with the nominative and with light stress on *ṣadaqa*, making *ẓannuhu* a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimāl*) from *Iblīsu*.

It was said: This verse is specific to the people of Saba'. The meaning is that they changed and altered after having believed in what their messengers brought. It was also said: It is general, i.e., Iblis's assumption was confirmed about all people except those who obey God. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misguided them they would obey him, so his assumption was confirmed and they followed him. Al-Hasan said: He did not strike them with a whip or sticks; rather, he assumed an assumption through his whispering.

The accusative of ﴿except a group of the believers﴾ is an exception (*istithnā'*), and in it there are two views. The first is that it means some of the believers, because many believers commit sins and yield to Iblis in some acts of disobedience, and only a group were spared from him, and they are those about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Hijr: 42; al-Isra': 65). It was also said that the intended meaning of ﴿a group of the believers﴾ is all the believers, with *min* being explicative (*bayāniyya*).

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e., he had no power to dominate them, meaning he did not compel them to disbelief; rather, his part was only calling and whispering and adorning. It was said: *sulṭān* means power and strength; it was also said: proof. The exception in His saying: ﴿except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾ is disjunct (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: he has no authority over them, but We tested them with his whispering so that We might know.

It was also said that it is connected and exhaustive (*muttaṣil mufarragh*) from the most general of the general (*min aʿamm al-ʿāmm*), i.e., he had no domination over them in any state and for no reason, except so that the one who believes may be distinguished from the one who does not believe, for He, glorified is He, had known that with eternal knowledge.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "except that We may know that among you." It was said: "except that you may know," and it was said: "that Our allies and the angels may know."

Al-Zuhri recited *illā li-yuʿlama* in the passive voice. The preferable interpretation of knowledge here is as distinguishing and manifesting, as we mentioned. ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., Watcher over them. Muqatil said: He knows everything, of faith and doubt.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *ḥasan*), al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and others narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I not fight those among my people who turned back, together with those who came forward?" He permitted me to fight them and commanded me. When I left him, he sent after me and called me back, and said: "Call the people. Whoever among them accepts Islam, accept it from him; and whoever does not accept Islam, do not hasten until I have written to you, and what was revealed about Saba' was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Saba'? Is it a land or a woman?" He said: "It is neither a land nor a woman, but a man who fathered ten of the Arabs. Six of them went to the right (*tayammana*), and four went to the left (*tashā'ama*). As for those who went to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, and ʿĀmila. As for those who went to the right: al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Himyar, Kinda, Madhhij, and Anmar." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Anmar?" He said: "Those among them are Khath'am and Bajila."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn ʿAdi, al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, but more concise.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿the flood of al-ʿArim﴾, that he said: "The strong one."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "The flood of al-ʿArim was a valley in Yemen that flowed toward Makkah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿bitter fruit (*ukulin khamṭ*)﴾, that he said: "It is the arak tree."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ that he said: "That is the scrutiny (*munāqasha*)."

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We placed between them﴾, meaning between their dwellings, ﴿and between the towns which We had blessed﴾, meaning the holy land, ﴿visible towns﴾, meaning populated and fertile, ﴿and We determined therein the journey﴾, meaning between their dwellings and the land of the Levant, ﴿Travel therein﴾ when they set out from their homes to the land of the Levant, the holy land.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed Iblis confirmed his assumption about them﴾, that he said: "Iblis said: Indeed Adam was created from dust, from clay, and from black mud molded, a weak creation, and I was created from fire, and fire burns everything. I will surely seize his descendants, except a few." He said: "So he confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except a group of the believers." He said: "They are all the believers."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of some of those who give thanks for His blessings, He followed it with the condition of some who deny them. So He said: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba a sign in their dwelling place﴾. What is meant by Sheba is the tribe descended from Sheba, who was Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn Hud.

The majority of reciters read *li-Saba'in* with a kasrah and tanwin, treating it as the name of a people, meaning the group who are the descendants of Saba'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *li-Saba'* without tanwin, as a diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*), by interpreting it as a tribe. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The first reading is supported by His saying *fi masakinihim* (in their dwelling places). Had it been understood as a tribe, it would have said *fi masakinihā* (in its dwelling places). The first reading is attested in the verse of the poet:

> The arrivals, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
> the buffalo hides have bitten their necks.

Also attested for the second reading is the verse of the poet:

> Of Saba', the present ones, Ma'rib, when
> they build, apart from its channel, the dam.

Qunbul, Abu Haywah and al-Jahdari read *li-Saba'* with a sukun on the hamzah, and it has also been read with the hamzah changed into an alif.

The majority read *fi masakinihim* in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, and the reason for preferring it is that they had many dwellings and numerous homes. Hamzah and Hafs read it in the singular with a fathah on the kaf.

Al-Kisa'i read it in the singular with a kasrah on the kaf. This reading was also read by Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash. The justification for the singular is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that covers the few and the many, or it is a noun of place used with the sense of the plural. These dwellings that they had are the ones now called Ma'rib, and between it and Sana'a is a journey of three nights. The meaning of His saying *ayah* (a sign) is a proof, a clear indication of the perfection of Allah's power and the wonder of His craftsmanship. Then He explained this sign, saying: ﴿two gardens, on the right and on the left﴾. Their raising (*irtfa'uhuma*) is either as an apposition (*badal*) of *ayah*, as al-Farra' said, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Zajjaj said, or as the subject whose predicate is ﴿on the right and on the left﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this last view, but it has the problem that it is not permissible to begin with an indefinite noun without a justification (*musawwigh*).

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *jannatayn* in the accusative, treating it as a second predicate, with *ayah* as its subject. These two gardens were on the right and the left of their valley and surrounded it from both of its sides. Their dwellings were in the valley, and the sign was the two gardens. A woman would walk between them with a basket on her head, and it would fill with all kinds of fruit that fell down without her touching it with her hand.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the sign that was for the people of Sheba in their dwellings was that they did not see in them a gnat, a fly, a flea, a louse, a scorpion, a snake, or any other vermin. When a caravan came to them with lice in their clothes, the lice died upon seeing their houses.

Al-Qushayri said: He did not mean two gardens only, but that on both sides, to the right and the left, on each side there were many orchards. ﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord﴾: that is, it was said to them, and there was no command in the strict sense, but the intended meaning is that they were enabled to enjoy those blessings. It is also said that the angels said this to them. The provision is the fruits of the two gardens. It is also said that they were addressed this way through their prophet, and [the verse means]: and give thanks to Him for what He has provided you of these blessings, and act in obedience to Him and avoid His disobedience. The clause ﴿a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ is a new sentence (*mustanfa'ah*) explaining the reason that requires gratitude.

The meaning: this is a good land because of the abundance of its trees and the goodness of its fruits. It is also said that the meaning of its being good is that it is not salt-marshy (*sabkhah*). It is also said that there are no vermin in it. Mujahid said: it is Sana'a. The meaning of ﴿and a forgiving Lord﴾ is that the Bestower of blessings upon them is a forgiving Lord for their sins. Muqatil said: the meaning is, "and your Lord, if you give thanks for what He provided you in it, is a forgiving Lord of sins." It is also said that He combined for them the goodness of the land and forgiveness only to indicate that provision may contain something unlawful.

Warsh read *baldatun* and *rabbun* in the accusative, as a form of praise, or by supposing "dwell in a land and give thanks to a Lord."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they did after this blessing with which He had favored them. So He said: ﴿but they turned away﴾ from giving thanks, and ﴿disbelieved in Allah and denied their messengers﴾. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to the people of Sheba thirteen prophets, and they denied them. Wahb said the same.

Then, when they turned away from giving thanks for the blessing, Allah sent upon them a punishment by which He stripped them of what He had bestowed upon them. So He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim﴾. This was because the water used to come to the land of Sheba from the valleys of Yemen. They built a dam (*radm*) between two mountains and held the water back, and in that dam they made three gates, one above another. They used to irrigate from the upper gate, then the second, then the third, and so they became fertile and their wealth increased. When they denied their messengers, Allah sent a rat which gnawed through that dam until it broke, and the water entered their gardens and drowned them, and the flood buried their houses. This is the flood of al-Arim. *Al-'Arim* is the plural of *'arimah*, which is the dam that holds back the water. Qatadah and others said the same.

Al-Suddi said: *al-'Arim* is a name for the dam. The meaning is: We sent upon them the flood of the dam, the 'Arim. 'Ata' said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the valley.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the rat that breached the dam for them, which is called *al-Khuld*. The flood was attributed to it because it was the cause of its flow. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-'Arim* is one of the names of the mouse. Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih said: *al-'Arim* is red water which Allah sent into the dam, and it split and destroyed it. It is also said that *al-'Arim* is the name of heavy rain, and it is also said that it is the name of a violent flood. The root meaning of *al-'irامah* is strength, harshness and difficulty. One says: *'arama* so-and-so, when he became severe and difficult.

It is reported from Ibn al-A'rabi that he said: *al-'Arim* is the flood that cannot be withstood.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-'Arim* is everything that is a barrier between two things.

﴿And We exchanged for them their two gardens for two gardens﴾: that is, We destroyed their two gardens which contained those good fruits and fine varieties, and We gave them in their place two gardens with nothing good in them, and no benefit for them from what grew in them. For this reason He said: ﴿of bitter produce (*dhawatay ukulin khamt*)﴾. The majority read *ukulin* with tanwin and without its being annexed to *khamt*. Abu 'Amr read it with annexation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-khamt* is the tamarisk (*arak*), and many of the exegetes said the same.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-khamt* is every bitter tree with thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: every plant in which there is bitterness that cannot be eaten.

Al-Mubarrad said: everything that changed into something not desired is called *khamt*, and from this comes milk when it has turned. The reading of the majority is preferable to that of Abu 'Amr.

*Khamt* is an attribute of *ukul* or an apposition to it, because *ukul* is itself the *khamt*.

Al-Akhfash said: the annexation is better in Arabic usage, like "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*) and "a house of brick" (*dar ajurr*). The better interpretation of *khamt* is what al-Khalil and those with him mentioned.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-khamt* is a kind of tamarisk that has a edible fruit. Calling the substitute "two gardens" is by way of matching (*mushakalah*) or mockery of them. *Al-athl* is the well-known tree resembling the tamarisk (*tarfa'*), so said al-Farra' and others. He said: except that it is taller than the tamarisk. Its singular is *athalah* and its plural *athalat*.

Al-Hasan said: *al-athl* is wood. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the *nutar* tree. The first view is preferable, and the *athl* has no fruit.

*Al-sidr* is a well-known tree. Al-Farra' said: it is the *samur*. Al-Azhari said: there are two kinds of *sidr* tree: a wild one from which no benefit is taken and which is not suitable for washing, and which has a bitter fruit that is not eaten, and this is what is called *al-dall*. The second is the *sidr* that grows on water, whose fruit is the *nabq* (jujube), and whose leaf is a washing agent, resembling the *'unnab* tree.

It has been said: He described the *sidr* as "few" because among it there is a kind whose fruit is good to eat, and this is the second kind mentioned by al-Azhari.

Qatadah said: while their trees were among the best trees, Allah changed them into the worst of trees because of their deeds, so He destroyed their fruit-bearing trees and grew in their place *arak*, tamarisk, and *sidr*.

It is possible that His saying *qalil* (few) refers to all that was mentioned: the *khamt*, the *athl* and the *sidr*.

The indication in His saying *dhalika* (that) refers to what has preceded of the exchange, or to the verbal noun of *jazaynahum*. The *ba'* in *bima kafaru* is causal: that is, that exchange, or that recompense, is because of their disbelief in the blessing by turning away from giving thanks for it. ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾: that is, Do We requite this recompense, by stripping the blessing and sending down the punishment, except the one who is extremely ungrateful and excessive in it?

The majority read *yujazi* with a *ya'* vowelled with a *dammah* and the *za'* with a *fathah*, in the passive voice. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with *nun* and a *kasrah* on the *za'*, in the active voice, with Allah as the agent, glory be to Him. The word *al-kafur* is in the nominative under the first reading and in the accusative under the second. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the second reading, and said: because before it is *jazaynahum* (We requited them). The apparent meaning of the verse is that He requites none but the ungrateful, though the people of disobedience are also requited. Some people said the meaning of the verse is: He does not inflict this recompense, which is uprooting and destruction, except upon one who has disbelieved.

Mujahid said: the believer has his sins expiated, while the disbeliever is requited for every deed he did.

Tawus said: it is the scrutiny of the reckoning, but the believer is not scrutinized.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that He requites the disbeliever with an equal recompense, one like for like. Al-Nahhas preferred this answer.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed a number of visible towns﴾. This is coordinated with His saying ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾: that is, and it was part of their story that We placed between them and the towns We had blessed with water and trees. These towns are the towns of the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿Towns visible (qura zahirah)﴾: that is, continuous, one after another. Their trade route ran from their land, which is Ma'rib, to al-Sham. They would spend the night in one town and take their midday rest in another until they returned, and they had no need to carry provisions from their land to al-Sham. So this is part of the narrative of what Allah bestowed upon them.

Al-Hasan said: these towns were between Yemen and al-Sham. It was said that they numbered 4,700 towns. It was also said they were between Medina and al-Sham.

Al-Mubarrad said: the "visible towns" are well known, and they were called visible because of their visibility: when you leave one, the next one appears to you, so they were visible towns, that is, well known. One says: this is a visible matter, meaning a known matter.

﴿And We determined within them the journeying (al-sayr)﴾: that is, We made the journey from one town to another a single fixed measure, and that was half a day, as the exegetes said. Al-Farra' said: that is, We placed between each two towns half a day's journey, so that the midday rest would be in one town and the night in another, until one reached al-Sham. A person exerts himself in travel only for lack of provisions, water, and fear of the road. When provisions and security are available, he does not burden himself with hardship, but stops wherever he wishes.

The summary: Allah, glory be to Him, enumerated the blessings for them, then mentioned the calamities that befell them, then returned to enumerate the remaining blessings He had bestowed on them, which lie outside their land, namely the connection of towns between them and the places to which they wished to travel. Then after that He mentioned their being exchanged for deserts and wastelands, as will come. His saying ﴿Travel therein﴾ is on the assumption of a saying: that is, and We said to them, "Travel in those connected towns." It is a command of enablement: that is, and We enabled them to travel in them whenever they wished. ﴿Nights and days, secure﴾ from what they feared. The accusative of *layali* and *ayyaman* is adverbial of time (*zarfiyyah*), and the accusative of *aminin* is a circumstantial (*hal*).

Qatadah said: they used to travel without fear, nor hungry nor thirsty. They used to travel a distance of four months in security; no one would harm another, and even if a man met the killer of his father, he would not touch him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that they did not give thanks for the blessing but sought hardship and toil: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart."﴾ This utterance from them was out of insolence and transgression, since they grew weary of the blessing and did not endure well-being. So they wished for long journeys and for distance between their homelands, and they asked God, exalted is He, to place between them and the Levant, in place of those closely connected villages abundant in water, trees, and security, deserts, wastelands, and open plains with widely separated regions. God granted them their request, destroyed those closely connected villages, and took away the good, the water, and the trees that were in them. Their supplication was thus like the supplication of the Children of Israel, when they said: ﴿Then call upon your Lord for us that He bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 61), in place of the manna and the quails, and like the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and so on.

The majority of readers recited *Rabbana* with a fatha (*naṣb*), as a vocative construction (*munada mudaf*, a vocative noun followed by a genitive construction, i.e., "O our Lord"), and they also recited *bā'id* (as an imperative). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited *ba'id* with a shadda on the ʿayn (*bayyid*, intensive form). Ibn al-Sumayfa recited it with a ḍamma on the ʿayn as a past-tense verb (*buʿida*), so the meaning of this reading is complaint about the distance of the journeys. Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu al-ʿĀliya, Nasr ibn ʿĀsim, and Yaʿqub recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma (as the subject) and *baʿada* (with a fatha on the ʿayn) as a past-tense verb, in the construction of *mubtada'* and *khabar* (subject and predicate), meaning: "Our Lord has put far apart the distances of our journeys." This reading is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it, saying: "They only asked for something closer than that nearness which existed between them and the Levant through the closely connected villages, out of insolence, arrogance, and ingratitude for the blessing."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma and *baʿʿada* with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda, so the meaning of this reading is complaint that their Lord had made the distances between their journeys far apart, although they were close and connected by villages, trees, and water; this would then be part of their insolence. The brother of al-Hasan al-Basri recited, like the earlier reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa, but with *bayna* in the nominative as the subject (*fāʿil*), as is said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bond has been severed﴾ (al-Anʿam: 94). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj transmitted a reading similar to this one, but with *bayna* in the accusative as an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), with the estimate: "Our journey has become far, between our journeys."

Al-Nahhas said: When these readings differ in meaning, it is not permissible to say that one of them is better than the other, just as one does not say that about isolated reports (*akhbar al-ahad*) when their meanings differ. Rather, He informed about them that they asked their Lord to make the distance between their journeys far, and when He did that to them, they complained and were harmed. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, by disbelieving in God, being insolent toward His blessing, and exposing themselves to His punishment. ﴿So We made them narrations﴾, so that people speak of their news.

The meaning is: We made them people of stories that those after them would tell, in wonder at their deed and taking lesson from their condition and their end. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾, i.e., We scattered them in every direction through the lands, completely scattering them. This clause explains "made them narrations." When God, glorified is He, drowned their place and took away their garden, they dispersed throughout the lands, and the Arabs came to use them as proverbs, saying: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'" (*tafarraqū ayādī Sabā'*).

Al-Sha'bi said: So the Ansar joined Yathrib, Ghassan went to the Levant, the Azd went to ʿUmān, and Khuza'a went to Tihama.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story and what God did to them, are clear signs and manifest indications ﴿for every steadfast, grateful one﴾, i.e., for everyone who is greatly patient and grateful. He specified *ṣabbār shakūr* (steadfast and grateful) because they are the ones who benefit from admonitions and signs.

﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾. The majority recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress and *Iblīsu* in the nominative and *ẓannahu* in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), i.e., he confirmed about them an assumption that he assumed, or he was right in his assumption, or it is in the adverbial sense (*ẓarf*). The meaning is that he assumed about them that if he led them astray they would follow him, and he found them to be so. It may also be in the accusative as the object (*mafʿūl*), or with the removal of the preposition.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and ʿĀṣim recited *ṣaddaqa* with a shadda and *ẓannahu* in the accusative as its object. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: That is, he confirmed the assumption that he assumed. Mujahid said: He assumed an assumption and confirmed his assumption, so it was as he assumed. Abu Ja'far, Abu al-Jahja', al-Zuhri, and Zayd ibn ʿAli recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress, *Iblīsa* in the accusative, and *ẓannuhu* in the nominative. Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for this reading in my view, though al-Farra' permitted it, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it, making *al-ẓann* the subject of *ṣadaqa* and *Iblīs* its object. The meaning is that Iblis's assumption had embellished something for him regarding them, and his assumption was confirmed, as if he said: "And indeed the assumption of Iblis was confirmed concerning them." It was narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he recited both with the nominative and with light stress on *ṣadaqa*, making *ẓannuhu* a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimāl*) from *Iblīsu*.

It was said: This verse is specific to the people of Saba'. The meaning is that they changed and altered after having believed in what their messengers brought. It was also said: It is general, i.e., Iblis's assumption was confirmed about all people except those who obey God. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misguided them they would obey him, so his assumption was confirmed and they followed him. Al-Hasan said: He did not strike them with a whip or sticks; rather, he assumed an assumption through his whispering.

The accusative of ﴿except a group of the believers﴾ is an exception (*istithnā'*), and in it there are two views. The first is that it means some of the believers, because many believers commit sins and yield to Iblis in some acts of disobedience, and only a group were spared from him, and they are those about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Hijr: 42; al-Isra': 65). It was also said that the intended meaning of ﴿a group of the believers﴾ is all the believers, with *min* being explicative (*bayāniyya*).

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e., he had no power to dominate them, meaning he did not compel them to disbelief; rather, his part was only calling and whispering and adorning. It was said: *sulṭān* means power and strength; it was also said: proof. The exception in His saying: ﴿except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾ is disjunct (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: he has no authority over them, but We tested them with his whispering so that We might know.

It was also said that it is connected and exhaustive (*muttaṣil mufarragh*) from the most general of the general (*min aʿamm al-ʿāmm*), i.e., he had no domination over them in any state and for no reason, except so that the one who believes may be distinguished from the one who does not believe, for He, glorified is He, had known that with eternal knowledge.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "except that We may know that among you." It was said: "except that you may know," and it was said: "that Our allies and the angels may know."

Al-Zuhri recited *illā li-yuʿlama* in the passive voice. The preferable interpretation of knowledge here is as distinguishing and manifesting, as we mentioned. ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., Watcher over them. Muqatil said: He knows everything, of faith and doubt.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *ḥasan*), al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and others narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I not fight those among my people who turned back, together with those who came forward?" He permitted me to fight them and commanded me. When I left him, he sent after me and called me back, and said: "Call the people. Whoever among them accepts Islam, accept it from him; and whoever does not accept Islam, do not hasten until I have written to you, and what was revealed about Saba' was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Saba'? Is it a land or a woman?" He said: "It is neither a land nor a woman, but a man who fathered ten of the Arabs. Six of them went to the right (*tayammana*), and four went to the left (*tashā'ama*). As for those who went to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, and ʿĀmila. As for those who went to the right: al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Himyar, Kinda, Madhhij, and Anmar." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Anmar?" He said: "Those among them are Khath'am and Bajila."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn ʿAdi, al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, but more concise.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿the flood of al-ʿArim﴾, that he said: "The strong one."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "The flood of al-ʿArim was a valley in Yemen that flowed toward Makkah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿bitter fruit (*ukulin khamṭ*)﴾, that he said: "It is the arak tree."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ that he said: "That is the scrutiny (*munāqasha*)."

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We placed between them﴾, meaning between their dwellings, ﴿and between the towns which We had blessed﴾, meaning the holy land, ﴿visible towns﴾, meaning populated and fertile, ﴿and We determined therein the journey﴾, meaning between their dwellings and the land of the Levant, ﴿Travel therein﴾ when they set out from their homes to the land of the Levant, the holy land.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed Iblis confirmed his assumption about them﴾, that he said: "Iblis said: Indeed Adam was created from dust, from clay, and from black mud molded, a weak creation, and I was created from fire, and fire burns everything. I will surely seize his descendants, except a few." He said: "So he confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except a group of the believers." He said: "They are all the believers."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of some of those who give thanks for His blessings, He followed it with the condition of some who deny them. So He said: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba a sign in their dwelling place﴾. What is meant by Sheba is the tribe descended from Sheba, who was Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn Hud.

The majority of reciters read *li-Saba'in* with a kasrah and tanwin, treating it as the name of a people, meaning the group who are the descendants of Saba'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *li-Saba'* without tanwin, as a diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*), by interpreting it as a tribe. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The first reading is supported by His saying *fi masakinihim* (in their dwelling places). Had it been understood as a tribe, it would have said *fi masakinihā* (in its dwelling places). The first reading is attested in the verse of the poet:

> The arrivals, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
> the buffalo hides have bitten their necks.

Also attested for the second reading is the verse of the poet:

> Of Saba', the present ones, Ma'rib, when
> they build, apart from its channel, the dam.

Qunbul, Abu Haywah and al-Jahdari read *li-Saba'* with a sukun on the hamzah, and it has also been read with the hamzah changed into an alif.

The majority read *fi masakinihim* in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, and the reason for preferring it is that they had many dwellings and numerous homes. Hamzah and Hafs read it in the singular with a fathah on the kaf.

Al-Kisa'i read it in the singular with a kasrah on the kaf. This reading was also read by Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash. The justification for the singular is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that covers the few and the many, or it is a noun of place used with the sense of the plural. These dwellings that they had are the ones now called Ma'rib, and between it and Sana'a is a journey of three nights. The meaning of His saying *ayah* (a sign) is a proof, a clear indication of the perfection of Allah's power and the wonder of His craftsmanship. Then He explained this sign, saying: ﴿two gardens, on the right and on the left﴾. Their raising (*irtfa'uhuma*) is either as an apposition (*badal*) of *ayah*, as al-Farra' said, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Zajjaj said, or as the subject whose predicate is ﴿on the right and on the left﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this last view, but it has the problem that it is not permissible to begin with an indefinite noun without a justification (*musawwigh*).

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *jannatayn* in the accusative, treating it as a second predicate, with *ayah* as its subject. These two gardens were on the right and the left of their valley and surrounded it from both of its sides. Their dwellings were in the valley, and the sign was the two gardens. A woman would walk between them with a basket on her head, and it would fill with all kinds of fruit that fell down without her touching it with her hand.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the sign that was for the people of Sheba in their dwellings was that they did not see in them a gnat, a fly, a flea, a louse, a scorpion, a snake, or any other vermin. When a caravan came to them with lice in their clothes, the lice died upon seeing their houses.

Al-Qushayri said: He did not mean two gardens only, but that on both sides, to the right and the left, on each side there were many orchards. ﴿Eat from the provision of your Lord﴾: that is, it was said to them, and there was no command in the strict sense, but the intended meaning is that they were enabled to enjoy those blessings. It is also said that the angels said this to them. The provision is the fruits of the two gardens. It is also said that they were addressed this way through their prophet, and [the verse means]: and give thanks to Him for what He has provided you of these blessings, and act in obedience to Him and avoid His disobedience. The clause ﴿a good land and a forgiving Lord﴾ is a new sentence (*mustanfa'ah*) explaining the reason that requires gratitude.

The meaning: this is a good land because of the abundance of its trees and the goodness of its fruits. It is also said that the meaning of its being good is that it is not salt-marshy (*sabkhah*). It is also said that there are no vermin in it. Mujahid said: it is Sana'a. The meaning of ﴿and a forgiving Lord﴾ is that the Bestower of blessings upon them is a forgiving Lord for their sins. Muqatil said: the meaning is, "and your Lord, if you give thanks for what He provided you in it, is a forgiving Lord of sins." It is also said that He combined for them the goodness of the land and forgiveness only to indicate that provision may contain something unlawful.

Warsh read *baldatun* and *rabbun* in the accusative, as a form of praise, or by supposing "dwell in a land and give thanks to a Lord."

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they did after this blessing with which He had favored them. So He said: ﴿but they turned away﴾ from giving thanks, and ﴿disbelieved in Allah and denied their messengers﴾. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to the people of Sheba thirteen prophets, and they denied them. Wahb said the same.

Then, when they turned away from giving thanks for the blessing, Allah sent upon them a punishment by which He stripped them of what He had bestowed upon them. So He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim﴾. This was because the water used to come to the land of Sheba from the valleys of Yemen. They built a dam (*radm*) between two mountains and held the water back, and in that dam they made three gates, one above another. They used to irrigate from the upper gate, then the second, then the third, and so they became fertile and their wealth increased. When they denied their messengers, Allah sent a rat which gnawed through that dam until it broke, and the water entered their gardens and drowned them, and the flood buried their houses. This is the flood of al-Arim. *Al-'Arim* is the plural of *'arimah*, which is the dam that holds back the water. Qatadah and others said the same.

Al-Suddi said: *al-'Arim* is a name for the dam. The meaning is: We sent upon them the flood of the dam, the 'Arim. 'Ata' said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the valley.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the rat that breached the dam for them, which is called *al-Khuld*. The flood was attributed to it because it was the cause of its flow. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-'Arim* is one of the names of the mouse. Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih said: *al-'Arim* is red water which Allah sent into the dam, and it split and destroyed it. It is also said that *al-'Arim* is the name of heavy rain, and it is also said that it is the name of a violent flood. The root meaning of *al-'irامah* is strength, harshness and difficulty. One says: *'arama* so-and-so, when he became severe and difficult.

It is reported from Ibn al-A'rabi that he said: *al-'Arim* is the flood that cannot be withstood.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-'Arim* is everything that is a barrier between two things.

﴿And We exchanged for them their two gardens for two gardens﴾: that is, We destroyed their two gardens which contained those good fruits and fine varieties, and We gave them in their place two gardens with nothing good in them, and no benefit for them from what grew in them. For this reason He said: ﴿of bitter produce (*dhawatay ukulin khamt*)﴾. The majority read *ukulin* with tanwin and without its being annexed to *khamt*. Abu 'Amr read it with annexation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-khamt* is the tamarisk (*arak*), and many of the exegetes said the same.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-khamt* is every bitter tree with thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: every plant in which there is bitterness that cannot be eaten.

Al-Mubarrad said: everything that changed into something not desired is called *khamt*, and from this comes milk when it has turned. The reading of the majority is preferable to that of Abu 'Amr.

*Khamt* is an attribute of *ukul* or an apposition to it, because *ukul* is itself the *khamt*.

Al-Akhfash said: the annexation is better in Arabic usage, like "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*) and "a house of brick" (*dar ajurr*). The better interpretation of *khamt* is what al-Khalil and those with him mentioned.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-khamt* is a kind of tamarisk that has a edible fruit. Calling the substitute "two gardens" is by way of matching (*mushakalah*) or mockery of them. *Al-athl* is the well-known tree resembling the tamarisk (*tarfa'*), so said al-Farra' and others. He said: except that it is taller than the tamarisk. Its singular is *athalah* and its plural *athalat*.

Al-Hasan said: *al-athl* is wood. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the *nutar* tree. The first view is preferable, and the *athl* has no fruit.

*Al-sidr* is a well-known tree. Al-Farra' said: it is the *samur*. Al-Azhari said: there are two kinds of *sidr* tree: a wild one from which no benefit is taken and which is not suitable for washing, and which has a bitter fruit that is not eaten, and this is what is called *al-dall*. The second is the *sidr* that grows on water, whose fruit is the *nabq* (jujube), and whose leaf is a washing agent, resembling the *'unnab* tree.

It has been said: He described the *sidr* as "few" because among it there is a kind whose fruit is good to eat, and this is the second kind mentioned by al-Azhari.

Qatadah said: while their trees were among the best trees, Allah changed them into the worst of trees because of their deeds, so He destroyed their fruit-bearing trees and grew in their place *arak*, tamarisk, and *sidr*.

It is possible that His saying *qalil* (few) refers to all that was mentioned: the *khamt*, the *athl* and the *sidr*.

The indication in His saying *dhalika* (that) refers to what has preceded of the exchange, or to the verbal noun of *jazaynahum*. The *ba'* in *bima kafaru* is causal: that is, that exchange, or that recompense, is because of their disbelief in the blessing by turning away from giving thanks for it. ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾: that is, Do We requite this recompense, by stripping the blessing and sending down the punishment, except the one who is extremely ungrateful and excessive in it?

The majority read *yujazi* with a *ya'* vowelled with a *dammah* and the *za'* with a *fathah*, in the passive voice. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with *nun* and a *kasrah* on the *za'*, in the active voice, with Allah as the agent, glory be to Him. The word *al-kafur* is in the nominative under the first reading and in the accusative under the second. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the second reading, and said: because before it is *jazaynahum* (We requited them). The apparent meaning of the verse is that He requites none but the ungrateful, though the people of disobedience are also requited. Some people said the meaning of the verse is: He does not inflict this recompense, which is uprooting and destruction, except upon one who has disbelieved.

Mujahid said: the believer has his sins expiated, while the disbeliever is requited for every deed he did.

Tawus said: it is the scrutiny of the reckoning, but the believer is not scrutinized.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that He requites the disbeliever with an equal recompense, one like for like. Al-Nahhas preferred this answer.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed a number of visible towns﴾. This is coordinated with His saying ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾: that is, and it was part of their story that We placed between them and the towns We had blessed with water and trees. These towns are the towns of the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿Towns visible (qura zahirah)﴾: that is, continuous, one after another. Their trade route ran from their land, which is Ma'rib, to al-Sham. They would spend the night in one town and take their midday rest in another until they returned, and they had no need to carry provisions from their land to al-Sham. So this is part of the narrative of what Allah bestowed upon them.

Al-Hasan said: these towns were between Yemen and al-Sham. It was said that they numbered 4,700 towns. It was also said they were between Medina and al-Sham.

Al-Mubarrad said: the "visible towns" are well known, and they were called visible because of their visibility: when you leave one, the next one appears to you, so they were visible towns, that is, well known. One says: this is a visible matter, meaning a known matter.

﴿And We determined within them the journeying (al-sayr)﴾: that is, We made the journey from one town to another a single fixed measure, and that was half a day, as the exegetes said. Al-Farra' said: that is, We placed between each two towns half a day's journey, so that the midday rest would be in one town and the night in another, until one reached al-Sham. A person exerts himself in travel only for lack of provisions, water, and fear of the road. When provisions and security are available, he does not burden himself with hardship, but stops wherever he wishes.

The summary: Allah, glory be to Him, enumerated the blessings for them, then mentioned the calamities that befell them, then returned to enumerate the remaining blessings He had bestowed on them, which lie outside their land, namely the connection of towns between them and the places to which they wished to travel. Then after that He mentioned their being exchanged for deserts and wastelands, as will come. His saying ﴿Travel therein﴾ is on the assumption of a saying: that is, and We said to them, "Travel in those connected towns." It is a command of enablement: that is, and We enabled them to travel in them whenever they wished. ﴿Nights and days, secure﴾ from what they feared. The accusative of *layali* and *ayyaman* is adverbial of time (*zarfiyyah*), and the accusative of *aminin* is a circumstantial (*hal*).

Qatadah said: they used to travel without fear, nor hungry nor thirsty. They used to travel a distance of four months in security; no one would harm another, and even if a man met the killer of his father, he would not touch him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that they did not give thanks for the blessing but sought hardship and toil: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart."﴾ This utterance from them was out of insolence and transgression, since they grew weary of the blessing and did not endure well-being. So they wished for long journeys and for distance between their homelands, and they asked God, exalted is He, to place between them and the Levant, in place of those closely connected villages abundant in water, trees, and security, deserts, wastelands, and open plains with widely separated regions. God granted them their request, destroyed those closely connected villages, and took away the good, the water, and the trees that were in them. Their supplication was thus like the supplication of the Children of Israel, when they said: ﴿Then call upon your Lord for us that He bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 61), in place of the manna and the quails, and like the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and so on.

The majority of readers recited *Rabbana* with a fatha (*naṣb*), as a vocative construction (*munada mudaf*, a vocative noun followed by a genitive construction, i.e., "O our Lord"), and they also recited *bā'id* (as an imperative). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited *ba'id* with a shadda on the ʿayn (*bayyid*, intensive form). Ibn al-Sumayfa recited it with a ḍamma on the ʿayn as a past-tense verb (*buʿida*), so the meaning of this reading is complaint about the distance of the journeys. Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu al-ʿĀliya, Nasr ibn ʿĀsim, and Yaʿqub recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma (as the subject) and *baʿada* (with a fatha on the ʿayn) as a past-tense verb, in the construction of *mubtada'* and *khabar* (subject and predicate), meaning: "Our Lord has put far apart the distances of our journeys." This reading is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it, saying: "They only asked for something closer than that nearness which existed between them and the Levant through the closely connected villages, out of insolence, arrogance, and ingratitude for the blessing."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma and *baʿʿada* with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda, so the meaning of this reading is complaint that their Lord had made the distances between their journeys far apart, although they were close and connected by villages, trees, and water; this would then be part of their insolence. The brother of al-Hasan al-Basri recited, like the earlier reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa, but with *bayna* in the nominative as the subject (*fāʿil*), as is said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bond has been severed﴾ (al-Anʿam: 94). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj transmitted a reading similar to this one, but with *bayna* in the accusative as an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), with the estimate: "Our journey has become far, between our journeys."

Al-Nahhas said: When these readings differ in meaning, it is not permissible to say that one of them is better than the other, just as one does not say that about isolated reports (*akhbar al-ahad*) when their meanings differ. Rather, He informed about them that they asked their Lord to make the distance between their journeys far, and when He did that to them, they complained and were harmed. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, by disbelieving in God, being insolent toward His blessing, and exposing themselves to His punishment. ﴿So We made them narrations﴾, so that people speak of their news.

The meaning is: We made them people of stories that those after them would tell, in wonder at their deed and taking lesson from their condition and their end. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾, i.e., We scattered them in every direction through the lands, completely scattering them. This clause explains "made them narrations." When God, glorified is He, drowned their place and took away their garden, they dispersed throughout the lands, and the Arabs came to use them as proverbs, saying: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'" (*tafarraqū ayādī Sabā'*).

Al-Sha'bi said: So the Ansar joined Yathrib, Ghassan went to the Levant, the Azd went to ʿUmān, and Khuza'a went to Tihama.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story and what God did to them, are clear signs and manifest indications ﴿for every steadfast, grateful one﴾, i.e., for everyone who is greatly patient and grateful. He specified *ṣabbār shakūr* (steadfast and grateful) because they are the ones who benefit from admonitions and signs.

﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾. The majority recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress and *Iblīsu* in the nominative and *ẓannahu* in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), i.e., he confirmed about them an assumption that he assumed, or he was right in his assumption, or it is in the adverbial sense (*ẓarf*). The meaning is that he assumed about them that if he led them astray they would follow him, and he found them to be so. It may also be in the accusative as the object (*mafʿūl*), or with the removal of the preposition.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and ʿĀṣim recited *ṣaddaqa* with a shadda and *ẓannahu* in the accusative as its object. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: That is, he confirmed the assumption that he assumed. Mujahid said: He assumed an assumption and confirmed his assumption, so it was as he assumed. Abu Ja'far, Abu al-Jahja', al-Zuhri, and Zayd ibn ʿAli recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress, *Iblīsa* in the accusative, and *ẓannuhu* in the nominative. Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for this reading in my view, though al-Farra' permitted it, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it, making *al-ẓann* the subject of *ṣadaqa* and *Iblīs* its object. The meaning is that Iblis's assumption had embellished something for him regarding them, and his assumption was confirmed, as if he said: "And indeed the assumption of Iblis was confirmed concerning them." It was narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he recited both with the nominative and with light stress on *ṣadaqa*, making *ẓannuhu* a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimāl*) from *Iblīsu*.

It was said: This verse is specific to the people of Saba'. The meaning is that they changed and altered after having believed in what their messengers brought. It was also said: It is general, i.e., Iblis's assumption was confirmed about all people except those who obey God. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misguided them they would obey him, so his assumption was confirmed and they followed him. Al-Hasan said: He did not strike them with a whip or sticks; rather, he assumed an assumption through his whispering.

The accusative of ﴿except a group of the believers﴾ is an exception (*istithnā'*), and in it there are two views. The first is that it means some of the believers, because many believers commit sins and yield to Iblis in some acts of disobedience, and only a group were spared from him, and they are those about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Hijr: 42; al-Isra': 65). It was also said that the intended meaning of ﴿a group of the believers﴾ is all the believers, with *min* being explicative (*bayāniyya*).

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e., he had no power to dominate them, meaning he did not compel them to disbelief; rather, his part was only calling and whispering and adorning. It was said: *sulṭān* means power and strength; it was also said: proof. The exception in His saying: ﴿except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾ is disjunct (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: he has no authority over them, but We tested them with his whispering so that We might know.

It was also said that it is connected and exhaustive (*muttaṣil mufarragh*) from the most general of the general (*min aʿamm al-ʿāmm*), i.e., he had no domination over them in any state and for no reason, except so that the one who believes may be distinguished from the one who does not believe, for He, glorified is He, had known that with eternal knowledge.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "except that We may know that among you." It was said: "except that you may know," and it was said: "that Our allies and the angels may know."

Al-Zuhri recited *illā li-yuʿlama* in the passive voice. The preferable interpretation of knowledge here is as distinguishing and manifesting, as we mentioned. ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., Watcher over them. Muqatil said: He knows everything, of faith and doubt.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *ḥasan*), al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and others narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I not fight those among my people who turned back, together with those who came forward?" He permitted me to fight them and commanded me. When I left him, he sent after me and called me back, and said: "Call the people. Whoever among them accepts Islam, accept it from him; and whoever does not accept Islam, do not hasten until I have written to you, and what was revealed about Saba' was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Saba'? Is it a land or a woman?" He said: "It is neither a land nor a woman, but a man who fathered ten of the Arabs. Six of them went to the right (*tayammana*), and four went to the left (*tashā'ama*). As for those who went to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, and ʿĀmila. As for those who went to the right: al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Himyar, Kinda, Madhhij, and Anmar." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Anmar?" He said: "Those among them are Khath'am and Bajila."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn ʿAdi, al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, but more concise.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿the flood of al-ʿArim﴾, that he said: "The strong one."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "The flood of al-ʿArim was a valley in Yemen that flowed toward Makkah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿bitter fruit (*ukulin khamṭ*)﴾, that he said: "It is the arak tree."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ that he said: "That is the scrutiny (*munāqasha*)."

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We placed between them﴾, meaning between their dwellings, ﴿and between the towns which We had blessed﴾, meaning the holy land, ﴿visible towns﴾, meaning populated and fertile, ﴿and We determined therein the journey﴾, meaning between their dwellings and the land of the Levant, ﴿Travel therein﴾ when they set out from their homes to the land of the Levant, the holy land.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed Iblis confirmed his assumption about them﴾, that he said: "Iblis said: Indeed Adam was created from dust, from clay, and from black mud molded, a weak creation, and I was created from fire, and fire burns everything. I will surely seize his descendants, except a few." He said: "So he confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except a group of the believers." He said: "They are all the believers."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of some of those who give thanks for His blessings, He followed it with the condition of some who deny them. So He said: ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba a sign in their dwelling place﴾. What is meant by Sheba is the tribe descended from Sheba, who was Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn Hud.

The majority of reciters read *li-Saba'in* with a kasrah and tanwin, treating it as the name of a people, meaning the group who are the descendants of Saba'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *li-Saba'* without tanwin, as a diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*), by interpreting it as a tribe. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The first reading is supported by His saying *fi masakinihim* (in their dwelling places). Had it been understood as a tribe, it would have said *fi masakinihā* (in its dwelling places). The first reading is attested in the verse of the poet:

> The arrivals, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
> the buffalo hides have bitten their necks.

Also attested for the second reading is the verse of the poet:

> Of Saba', the present ones, Ma'rib, when
> they build, apart from its channel, the dam.

Qunbul, Abu Haywah and al-Jahdari read *li-Saba'* with a sukun on the hamzah, and it has also been read with the hamzah changed into an alif.

The majority read *fi masakinihim* in the plural. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, and the reason for preferring it is that they had many dwellings and numerous homes. Hamzah and Hafs read it in the singular with a fathah on the kaf.

Al-Kisa'i read it in the singular with a kasrah on the kaf. This reading was also read by Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash. The justification for the singular is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that covers the few and the many, or it is a noun of place used with the sense of the plural. These dwellings that they had are the ones now called Ma'rib, and between it and Sana'a is a journey of three nights. The meaning of His saying *ayah* (a sign) is a proof, a clear indication of the perfection of Allah's power and the wonder of His craftsmanship. Then He explained this sign, saying: ﴿two gardens, on the right and on the left﴾. Their raising (*irtfa'uhuma*) is either as an apposition (*badal*) of *ayah*, as al-Farra' said, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Zajjaj said, or as the subject whose predicate is ﴿on the right and on the left﴾. Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this last view, but it has the problem that it is not permissible to begin with an indefinite noun without a justification (*musawwigh*).

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *jannatayn* in the accusative, treating it as a second predicate, with *ayah* as its subject.
