Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they did after this blessing with which He had favored them. So He said: ﴿but they turned away﴾ from giving thanks, and ﴿disbelieved in Allah and denied their messengers﴾. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to the people of Sheba thirteen prophets, and they denied them. Wahb said the same.

Then, when they turned away from giving thanks for the blessing, Allah sent upon them a punishment by which He stripped them of what He had bestowed upon them. So He said: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim﴾. This was because the water used to come to the land of Sheba from the valleys of Yemen. They built a dam (*radm*) between two mountains and held the water back, and in that dam they made three gates, one above another. They used to irrigate from the upper gate, then the second, then the third, and so they became fertile and their wealth increased. When they denied their messengers, Allah sent a rat which gnawed through that dam until it broke, and the water entered their gardens and drowned them, and the flood buried their houses. This is the flood of al-Arim. *Al-'Arim* is the plural of *'arimah*, which is the dam that holds back the water. Qatadah and others said the same.

Al-Suddi said: *al-'Arim* is a name for the dam. The meaning is: We sent upon them the flood of the dam, the 'Arim. 'Ata' said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the valley.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'Arim* is the name of the rat that breached the dam for them, which is called *al-Khuld*. The flood was attributed to it because it was the cause of its flow. Ibn al-A'rabi said: *al-'Arim* is one of the names of the mouse. Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih said: *al-'Arim* is red water which Allah sent into the dam, and it split and destroyed it. It is also said that *al-'Arim* is the name of heavy rain, and it is also said that it is the name of a violent flood. The root meaning of *al-'irامah* is strength, harshness and difficulty. One says: *'arama* so-and-so, when he became severe and difficult.

It is reported from Ibn al-A'rabi that he said: *al-'Arim* is the flood that cannot be withstood.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-'Arim* is everything that is a barrier between two things.

﴿And We exchanged for them their two gardens for two gardens﴾: that is, We destroyed their two gardens which contained those good fruits and fine varieties, and We gave them in their place two gardens with nothing good in them, and no benefit for them from what grew in them. For this reason He said: ﴿of bitter produce (*dhawatay ukulin khamt*)﴾. The majority read *ukulin* with tanwin and without its being annexed to *khamt*. Abu 'Amr read it with annexation.

Al-Khalil said: *al-khamt* is the tamarisk (*arak*), and many of the exegetes said the same.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-khamt* is every bitter tree with thorns.

Al-Zajjaj said: every plant in which there is bitterness that cannot be eaten.

Al-Mubarrad said: everything that changed into something not desired is called *khamt*, and from this comes milk when it has turned. The reading of the majority is preferable to that of Abu 'Amr.

*Khamt* is an attribute of *ukul* or an apposition to it, because *ukul* is itself the *khamt*.

Al-Akhfash said: the annexation is better in Arabic usage, like "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*) and "a house of brick" (*dar ajurr*). The better interpretation of *khamt* is what al-Khalil and those with him mentioned.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-khamt* is a kind of tamarisk that has a edible fruit. Calling the substitute "two gardens" is by way of matching (*mushakalah*) or mockery of them. *Al-athl* is the well-known tree resembling the tamarisk (*tarfa'*), so said al-Farra' and others. He said: except that it is taller than the tamarisk. Its singular is *athalah* and its plural *athalat*.

Al-Hasan said: *al-athl* is wood. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is the *nutar* tree. The first view is preferable, and the *athl* has no fruit.

*Al-sidr* is a well-known tree. Al-Farra' said: it is the *samur*. Al-Azhari said: there are two kinds of *sidr* tree: a wild one from which no benefit is taken and which is not suitable for washing, and which has a bitter fruit that is not eaten, and this is what is called *al-dall*. The second is the *sidr* that grows on water, whose fruit is the *nabq* (jujube), and whose leaf is a washing agent, resembling the *'unnab* tree.

It has been said: He described the *sidr* as "few" because among it there is a kind whose fruit is good to eat, and this is the second kind mentioned by al-Azhari.

Qatadah said: while their trees were among the best trees, Allah changed them into the worst of trees because of their deeds, so He destroyed their fruit-bearing trees and grew in their place *arak*, tamarisk, and *sidr*.

It is possible that His saying *qalil* (few) refers to all that was mentioned: the *khamt*, the *athl* and the *sidr*.

The indication in His saying *dhalika* (that) refers to what has preceded of the exchange, or to the verbal noun of *jazaynahum*. The *ba'* in *bima kafaru* is causal: that is, that exchange, or that recompense, is because of their disbelief in the blessing by turning away from giving thanks for it. ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾: that is, Do We requite this recompense, by stripping the blessing and sending down the punishment, except the one who is extremely ungrateful and excessive in it?

The majority read *yujazi* with a *ya'* vowelled with a *dammah* and the *za'* with a *fathah*, in the passive voice. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read it with *nun* and a *kasrah* on the *za'*, in the active voice, with Allah as the agent, glory be to Him. The word *al-kafur* is in the nominative under the first reading and in the accusative under the second. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the second reading, and said: because before it is *jazaynahum* (We requited them). The apparent meaning of the verse is that He requites none but the ungrateful, though the people of disobedience are also requited. Some people said the meaning of the verse is: He does not inflict this recompense, which is uprooting and destruction, except upon one who has disbelieved.

Mujahid said: the believer has his sins expiated, while the disbeliever is requited for every deed he did.

Tawus said: it is the scrutiny of the reckoning, but the believer is not scrutinized.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that He requites the disbeliever with an equal recompense, one like for like. Al-Nahhas preferred this answer.

﴿And We placed between them and the towns that We had blessed a number of visible towns﴾. This is coordinated with His saying ﴿Indeed there was for Sheba﴾: that is, and it was part of their story that We placed between them and the towns We had blessed with water and trees. These towns are the towns of the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿Towns visible (qura zahirah)﴾: that is, continuous, one after another. Their trade route ran from their land, which is Ma'rib, to al-Sham. They would spend the night in one town and take their midday rest in another until they returned, and they had no need to carry provisions from their land to al-Sham. So this is part of the narrative of what Allah bestowed upon them.

Al-Hasan said: these towns were between Yemen and al-Sham. It was said that they numbered 4,700 towns. It was also said they were between Medina and al-Sham.

Al-Mubarrad said: the "visible towns" are well known, and they were called visible because of their visibility: when you leave one, the next one appears to you, so they were visible towns, that is, well known. One says: this is a visible matter, meaning a known matter.

﴿And We determined within them the journeying (al-sayr)﴾: that is, We made the journey from one town to another a single fixed measure, and that was half a day, as the exegetes said. Al-Farra' said: that is, We placed between each two towns half a day's journey, so that the midday rest would be in one town and the night in another, until one reached al-Sham. A person exerts himself in travel only for lack of provisions, water, and fear of the road. When provisions and security are available, he does not burden himself with hardship, but stops wherever he wishes.

The summary: Allah, glory be to Him, enumerated the blessings for them, then mentioned the calamities that befell them, then returned to enumerate the remaining blessings He had bestowed on them, which lie outside their land, namely the connection of towns between them and the places to which they wished to travel. Then after that He mentioned their being exchanged for deserts and wastelands, as will come. His saying ﴿Travel therein﴾ is on the assumption of a saying: that is, and We said to them, "Travel in those connected towns." It is a command of enablement: that is, and We enabled them to travel in them whenever they wished. ﴿Nights and days, secure﴾ from what they feared. The accusative of *layali* and *ayyaman* is adverbial of time (*zarfiyyah*), and the accusative of *aminin* is a circumstantial (*hal*).

Qatadah said: they used to travel without fear, nor hungry nor thirsty. They used to travel a distance of four months in security; no one would harm another, and even if a man met the killer of his father, he would not touch him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned that they did not give thanks for the blessing but sought hardship and toil: ﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys far apart."﴾ This utterance from them was out of insolence and transgression, since they grew weary of the blessing and did not endure well-being. So they wished for long journeys and for distance between their homelands, and they asked God, exalted is He, to place between them and the Levant, in place of those closely connected villages abundant in water, trees, and security, deserts, wastelands, and open plains with widely separated regions. God granted them their request, destroyed those closely connected villages, and took away the good, the water, and the trees that were in them. Their supplication was thus like the supplication of the Children of Israel, when they said: ﴿Then call upon your Lord for us that He bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs...﴾ (al-Baqarah: 61), in place of the manna and the quails, and like the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ (al-Anfal: 32), and so on.

The majority of readers recited *Rabbana* with a fatha (*naṣb*), as a vocative construction (*munada mudaf*, a vocative noun followed by a genitive construction, i.e., "O our Lord"), and they also recited *bā'id* (as an imperative). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham from Ibn 'Amir recited *ba'id* with a shadda on the ʿayn (*bayyid*, intensive form). Ibn al-Sumayfa recited it with a ḍamma on the ʿayn as a past-tense verb (*buʿida*), so the meaning of this reading is complaint about the distance of the journeys. Abu Salih, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, Abu al-ʿĀliya, Nasr ibn ʿĀsim, and Yaʿqub recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma (as the subject) and *baʿada* (with a fatha on the ʿayn) as a past-tense verb, in the construction of *mubtada'* and *khabar* (subject and predicate), meaning: "Our Lord has put far apart the distances of our journeys." This reading is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hatim preferred it, saying: "They only asked for something closer than that nearness which existed between them and the Levant through the closely connected villages, out of insolence, arrogance, and ingratitude for the blessing."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and ʿĪsa ibn ʿUmar recited *Rabbuna* with a ḍamma and *baʿʿada* with a fatha on the ʿayn and a shadda, so the meaning of this reading is complaint that their Lord had made the distances between their journeys far apart, although they were close and connected by villages, trees, and water; this would then be part of their insolence. The brother of al-Hasan al-Basri recited, like the earlier reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa, but with *bayna* in the nominative as the subject (*fāʿil*), as is said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bond has been severed﴾ (al-Anʿam: 94). Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj transmitted a reading similar to this one, but with *bayna* in the accusative as an adverbial of place (*ẓarf*), with the estimate: "Our journey has become far, between our journeys."

Al-Nahhas said: When these readings differ in meaning, it is not permissible to say that one of them is better than the other, just as one does not say that about isolated reports (*akhbar al-ahad*) when their meanings differ. Rather, He informed about them that they asked their Lord to make the distance between their journeys far, and when He did that to them, they complained and were harmed. For this reason He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And they wronged themselves﴾, by disbelieving in God, being insolent toward His blessing, and exposing themselves to His punishment. ﴿So We made them narrations﴾, so that people speak of their news.

The meaning is: We made them people of stories that those after them would tell, in wonder at their deed and taking lesson from their condition and their end. ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾, i.e., We scattered them in every direction through the lands, completely scattering them. This clause explains "made them narrations." When God, glorified is He, drowned their place and took away their garden, they dispersed throughout the lands, and the Arabs came to use them as proverbs, saying: "They scattered like the hands of Saba'" (*tafarraqū ayādī Sabā'*).

Al-Sha'bi said: So the Ansar joined Yathrib, Ghassan went to the Levant, the Azd went to ʿUmān, and Khuza'a went to Tihama.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned of their story and what God did to them, are clear signs and manifest indications ﴿for every steadfast, grateful one﴾, i.e., for everyone who is greatly patient and grateful. He specified *ṣabbār shakūr* (steadfast and grateful) because they are the ones who benefit from admonitions and signs.

﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them﴾. The majority recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress and *Iblīsu* in the nominative and *ẓannahu* in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), i.e., he confirmed about them an assumption that he assumed, or he was right in his assumption, or it is in the adverbial sense (*ẓarf*). The meaning is that he assumed about them that if he led them astray they would follow him, and he found them to be so. It may also be in the accusative as the object (*mafʿūl*), or with the removal of the preposition.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and ʿĀṣim recited *ṣaddaqa* with a shadda and *ẓannahu* in the accusative as its object. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: That is, he confirmed the assumption that he assumed. Mujahid said: He assumed an assumption and confirmed his assumption, so it was as he assumed. Abu Ja'far, Abu al-Jahja', al-Zuhri, and Zayd ibn ʿAli recited *ṣadaqa* with light stress, *Iblīsa* in the accusative, and *ẓannuhu* in the nominative. Abu Hatim said: There is no basis for this reading in my view, though al-Farra' permitted it, and al-Zajjaj mentioned it, making *al-ẓann* the subject of *ṣadaqa* and *Iblīs* its object. The meaning is that Iblis's assumption had embellished something for him regarding them, and his assumption was confirmed, as if he said: "And indeed the assumption of Iblis was confirmed concerning them." It was narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he recited both with the nominative and with light stress on *ṣadaqa*, making *ẓannuhu* a substitute of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimāl*) from *Iblīsu*.

It was said: This verse is specific to the people of Saba'. The meaning is that they changed and altered after having believed in what their messengers brought. It was also said: It is general, i.e., Iblis's assumption was confirmed about all people except those who obey God. This was said by Mujahid and al-Hasan.

Al-Kalbi said: He assumed that if he led them astray they would answer him, and if he misguided them they would obey him, so his assumption was confirmed and they followed him. Al-Hasan said: He did not strike them with a whip or sticks; rather, he assumed an assumption through his whispering.

The accusative of ﴿except a group of the believers﴾ is an exception (*istithnā'*), and in it there are two views. The first is that it means some of the believers, because many believers commit sins and yield to Iblis in some acts of disobedience, and only a group were spared from him, and they are those about whom He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (al-Hijr: 42; al-Isra': 65). It was also said that the intended meaning of ﴿a group of the believers﴾ is all the believers, with *min* being explicative (*bayāniyya*).

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e., he had no power to dominate them, meaning he did not compel them to disbelief; rather, his part was only calling and whispering and adorning. It was said: *sulṭān* means power and strength; it was also said: proof. The exception in His saying: ﴿except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt about it﴾ is disjunct (*munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: he has no authority over them, but We tested them with his whispering so that We might know.

It was also said that it is connected and exhaustive (*muttaṣil mufarragh*) from the most general of the general (*min aʿamm al-ʿāmm*), i.e., he had no domination over them in any state and for no reason, except so that the one who believes may be distinguished from the one who does not believe, for He, glorified is He, had known that with eternal knowledge.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "except that We may know that among you." It was said: "except that you may know," and it was said: "that Our allies and the angels may know."

Al-Zuhri recited *illā li-yuʿlama* in the passive voice. The preferable interpretation of knowledge here is as distinguishing and manifesting, as we mentioned. ﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., Watcher over them. Muqatil said: He knows everything, of faith and doubt.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *ḥasan*), al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and others narrated from Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi who said: I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, shall I not fight those among my people who turned back, together with those who came forward?" He permitted me to fight them and commanded me. When I left him, he sent after me and called me back, and said: "Call the people. Whoever among them accepts Islam, accept it from him; and whoever does not accept Islam, do not hasten until I have written to you, and what was revealed about Saba' was revealed." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Saba'? Is it a land or a woman?" He said: "It is neither a land nor a woman, but a man who fathered ten of the Arabs. Six of them went to the right (*tayammana*), and four went to the left (*tashā'ama*). As for those who went to the left: Lakhm, Judham, Ghassan, and ʿĀmila. As for those who went to the right: al-Azd, al-Ash'ariyyun, Himyar, Kinda, Madhhij, and Anmar." A man said: "O Messenger of God, what is Anmar?" He said: "Those among them are Khath'am and Bajila."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tabarani, Ibn ʿAdi, al-Hakim (who graded it *ṣaḥīḥ*), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, but more concise.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿the flood of al-ʿArim﴾, that he said: "The strong one."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him: "The flood of al-ʿArim was a valley in Yemen that flowed toward Makkah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿bitter fruit (*ukulin khamṭ*)﴾, that he said: "It is the arak tree."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And do We requite except the ungrateful?﴾ that he said: "That is the scrutiny (*munāqasha*)."

Ishaq ibn Bishr and Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And We placed between them﴾, meaning between their dwellings, ﴿and between the towns which We had blessed﴾, meaning the holy land, ﴿visible towns﴾, meaning populated and fertile, ﴿and We determined therein the journey﴾, meaning between their dwellings and the land of the Levant, ﴿Travel therein﴾ when they set out from their homes to the land of the Levant, the holy land.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed Iblis confirmed his assumption about them﴾, that he said: "Iblis said: Indeed Adam was created from dust, from clay, and from black mud molded, a weak creation, and I was created from fire, and fire burns everything. I will surely seize his descendants, except a few." He said: "So he confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except a group of the believers." He said: "They are all the believers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 34, verses 22–27:

His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Allah﴾. This is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say this statement to the disbelievers of Quraysh, or to the disbelievers in general. The two objects of "claim" (zaʿamtum) are omitted, meaning: "whom you claimed to be gods," the context indicating them.

Muqatil said: It means, "Call upon them so that they may remove from you the harm which has befallen you in the years of hunger."

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, meaning: they have no power over good or evil, nor over bringing benefit or repelling harm in any matter whatsoever. He mentioned the heavens and the earth to intend generality, since they are the container of the existing things. ﴿And they have no share therein﴾, meaning: the deities have no partnership in the heavens and the earth, neither in creation, nor in ownership, nor in disposal. ﴿And for Him there is not among them any supporter﴾, meaning: for Allah, glorified is He, there is none among those deities who assists Him in any matter of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit﴾, meaning: the intercession of those who intercede with Him from among the angels and others. His saying: ﴿except for one whom He has permitted﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general circumstances, meaning: intercession does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for, from among the angels, the prophets, and their like from the people of knowledge and action. It is known that these do not intercede except for one who deserves intercession, not for the disbelievers. It is also possible that the meaning is: intercession from the intercessors qualified for it does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted, i.e., for his sake and concerning his matter, from among those deserving intercession on their behalf, not others who do not deserve it. The lam in "for whom" may be connected to the intercession itself.

Abu al-Baqa' said: as you say, "I interceded for him." It may also be connected to "benefit" (tanfaʿu), but the better view is that it is connected to the omitted element as we mentioned.

It has been said: What is meant by His saying, ﴿intercession does not benefit﴾ is that it does not exist at all except for one whom He has permitted. He attached the negation to its benefit rather than its occurrence, explicitly negating what was their purpose in its occurrence.

The majority read "adhina" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: Allah permitted him, since His name, glorified is He, is mentioned before this. Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, in the passive form, the one granting permission being Allah, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28].

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the fear of these intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, saying: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts﴾. The majority read "fuzzi'a" in the passive form, the agent being Allah, and the substitute for the agent being the prepositional phrase. Ibn ʿAmir read "fazza'a" in the active form, its subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He. Both readings have the doubled zay, and the form fa''ala (taf'īl) has the meaning of removal, so tafzīʿ is the removal of fear.

Al-Hasan read like the majority's reading, except that he lightened the zay.

Qutrub said: the meaning of ﴿removed from their hearts﴾ is: what was in them of terror, which is fear, was taken out.

Mujahid said: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning: intercession does not come from any of these worshipped ones other than Allah—from the angels, the prophets, or the idols—except that Allah, glorified is He, permits the angels, the prophets, and their like to intercede for whomever deserves it, and they are in the utmost fear of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they are in awe of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. When He permits them to intercede, they are struck with terror because of the tremendous matter that accompanies that state, and the intense fear lest something of Allah's decrees occur. When it is lifted from them, they say to the angels above them—and they are those who convey the revelation by permission—﴿What has your Lord said?﴾, meaning: what has He commanded? They say to them: He has said the truth, which is: accepting your intercession for those who deserve it, and not others. He is the Most High, the Great, so He may judge among His servants as He wills and do as He desires.

It has been said: this terror occurs to the angels at every command the Lord issues.

The meaning: intercession benefits only from the angels who, today, are in fear and obedient to Allah, not from inanimate things and devils.

It has also been said: those who say, "What has your Lord said?" are the ones being interceded for, and those who answer them are the intercessors from among the angels and prophets.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: until the terror is uncovered from the hearts of the polytheists in the Hereafter. The angels say to them: "What did your Lord say in the world?" They say: "The truth," and they confess at a time when confession will not benefit them.

Ibn ʿUmar and Qatadah read "farragha" with an unpointed ra and a pointed ghayn, from al-faraagh (emptiness). The meaning: Allah emptied their hearts, i.e., removed fear from them.

Ibn Mas'ud read "ifranqiʿa," with an unpointed ra after the fa', then a nun, then a qaf, then an unpointed ʿayn, from al-ifrinqiʿah, which means dispersal.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to rebuke and reprove the polytheists, saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: who bestows upon you these provisions from which you benefit? For your deities do not possess an atom's weight. Provision from the sky is rain and what is benefited from it, such as the sun, the moon and the stars; provision from the earth is plants, minerals and the like. Since the disbelievers were unable to answer this question, and their minds would not accept attributing this provision to their deities, and they might hesitate to attribute it to Allah for fear that the proof would be established against them, Allah commanded His Messenger to answer it, saying: ﴿Say: Allah﴾, i.e., it is He who provides for you from the heavens and the earth. Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to inform them that they are upon error—but in a fair manner regarding the argument, after the description of who is upon guidance and who is upon error had preceded. He said: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾. The meaning: one of the two groups—those who affirm Allah as the Creator and Provider and single Him out for worship, or those who worship inanimate things that cannot create, provide, benefit or harm—is indeed upon one of the two states, guidance or error. It is known to every intelligent person that whoever worships the One who creates, provides, benefits and harms is the one upon guidance, and whoever worships that which cannot create, provide, benefit or harm is the one upon error. Thus this statement has included the explanation of the party of guidance, who are the Muslims, and the party of error, who are the polytheists, in a manner more eloquent than explicit statement.

Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of this statement is the meaning of the words of one who is clear-sighted in argument to his companion: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he is the truthful, correct one and his companion the lying, mistaken one.

He said: "aw" (or), according to the Basrans, retains its own function and is not for doubt, but it is in the manner the Arabs use in such a context when the speaker does not wish to clarify while knowing the meaning.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it means "wa" (and), and its sense is: "Indeed we are upon guidance and you are in clear error," and from this is the verse of Jarir:

Do you think, Tha'labah of the horsemen, or Rabah, that they have equalled Tuhayyah and al-Rabab with them?

i.e., Tha'labah and Rabah. Likewise is the saying of another:

So when the severity of war intensified among us, we considered Rabah and Rizam.

i.e., and Rizam. His saying "aw iyyakum" is conjoined to the subject of "inna," and its predicate is the one mentioned; the predicate of the second is omitted for indication of it, i.e., "Indeed we are upon guidance or in clear error, and indeed you are upon guidance or in clear error." His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Allah﴾. This is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say this statement to the disbelievers of Quraysh, or to the disbelievers in general. The two objects of "claim" (zaʿamtum) are omitted, meaning: "whom you claimed to be gods," the context indicating them.

Muqatil said: It means, "Call upon them so that they may remove from you the harm which has befallen you in the years of hunger."

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, meaning: they have no power over good or evil, nor over bringing benefit or repelling harm in any matter whatsoever. He mentioned the heavens and the earth to intend generality, since they are the container of the existing things. ﴿And they have no share therein﴾, meaning: the deities have no partnership in the heavens and the earth, neither in creation, nor in ownership, nor in disposal. ﴿And for Him there is not among them any supporter﴾, meaning: for Allah, glorified is He, there is none among those deities who assists Him in any matter of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit﴾, meaning: the intercession of those who intercede with Him from among the angels and others. His saying: ﴿except for one whom He has permitted﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general circumstances, meaning: intercession does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for, from among the angels, the prophets, and their like from the people of knowledge and action. It is known that these do not intercede except for one who deserves intercession, not for the disbelievers. It is also possible that the meaning is: intercession from the intercessors qualified for it does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted, i.e., for his sake and concerning his matter, from among those deserving intercession on their behalf, not others who do not deserve it. The lam in "for whom" may be connected to the intercession itself.

Abu al-Baqa' said: as you say, "I interceded for him." It may also be connected to "benefit" (tanfaʿu), but the better view is that it is connected to the omitted element as we mentioned.

It has been said: What is meant by His saying, ﴿intercession does not benefit﴾ is that it does not exist at all except for one whom He has permitted. He attached the negation to its benefit rather than its occurrence, explicitly negating what was their purpose in its occurrence.

The majority read "adhina" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: Allah permitted him, since His name, glorified is He, is mentioned before this. Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, in the passive form, the one granting permission being Allah, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28].

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the fear of these intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, saying: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts﴾. The majority read "fuzzi'a" in the passive form, the agent being Allah, and the substitute for the agent being the prepositional phrase. Ibn ʿAmir read "fazza'a" in the active form, its subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He. Both readings have the doubled zay, and the form fa''ala (taf'īl) has the meaning of removal, so tafzīʿ is the removal of fear.

Al-Hasan read like the majority's reading, except that he lightened the zay.

Qutrub said: the meaning of ﴿removed from their hearts﴾ is: what was in them of terror, which is fear, was taken out.

Mujahid said: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning: intercession does not come from any of these worshipped ones other than Allah—from the angels, the prophets, or the idols—except that Allah, glorified is He, permits the angels, the prophets, and their like to intercede for whomever deserves it, and they are in the utmost fear of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they are in awe of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. When He permits them to intercede, they are struck with terror because of the tremendous matter that accompanies that state, and the intense fear lest something of Allah's decrees occur. When it is lifted from them, they say to the angels above them—and they are those who convey the revelation by permission—﴿What has your Lord said?﴾, meaning: what has He commanded? They say to them: He has said the truth, which is: accepting your intercession for those who deserve it, and not others. He is the Most High, the Great, so He may judge among His servants as He wills and do as He desires.

It has been said: this terror occurs to the angels at every command the Lord issues.

The meaning: intercession benefits only from the angels who, today, are in fear and obedient to Allah, not from inanimate things and devils.

It has also been said: those who say, "What has your Lord said?" are the ones being interceded for, and those who answer them are the intercessors from among the angels and prophets.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: until the terror is uncovered from the hearts of the polytheists in the Hereafter. The angels say to them: "What did your Lord say in the world?" They say: "The truth," and they confess at a time when confession will not benefit them.

Ibn ʿUmar and Qatadah read "farragha" with an unpointed ra and a pointed ghayn, from al-faraagh (emptiness). The meaning: Allah emptied their hearts, i.e., removed fear from them.

Ibn Mas'ud read "ifranqiʿa," with an unpointed ra after the fa', then a nun, then a qaf, then an unpointed ʿayn, from al-ifrinqiʿah, which means dispersal.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to rebuke and reprove the polytheists, saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: who bestows upon you these provisions from which you benefit? For your deities do not possess an atom's weight. Provision from the sky is rain and what is benefited from it, such as the sun, the moon and the stars; provision from the earth is plants, minerals and the like. He said: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾. He said: "aw" (or), according to the Basrans, retains its own function and is not for doubt, but it is in the manner the Arabs use in such a context when the speaker does not wish to clarify while knowing the meaning.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it means "wa" (and), and its sense is: "Indeed we are upon guidance and you are in clear error," and from this is the verse of Jarir:

Do you think, Tha'labah of the horsemen, or Rabah, that they have equalled Tuhayyah and al-Rabab with them?

i.e., Tha'labah and Rabah. Likewise is the saying of another:

The two objects of "claim" (zaʿamtum) are omitted, meaning: "whom you claimed to be gods," the context indicating them.

Muqatil said: It means, "Call upon them so that they may remove from you the harm which has befallen you in the years of hunger."

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, meaning: they have no power over good or evil, nor over bringing benefit or repelling harm in any matter whatsoever. He mentioned the heavens and the earth to intend generality, since they are the container of the existing things. ﴿And they have no share therein﴾, meaning: the deities have no partnership in the heavens and the earth, neither in creation, nor in ownership, nor in disposal. ﴿And for Him there is not among them any supporter﴾, meaning: for Allah, glorified is He, there is none among those deities who assists Him in any matter of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit﴾, meaning: the intercession of those who intercede with Him from among the angels and others. His saying: ﴿except for one whom He has permitted﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general circumstances, meaning: intercession does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for, from among the angels, the prophets, and their like from the people of knowledge and action. It is known that these do not intercede except for one who deserves intercession, not for the disbelievers. It is also possible that the meaning is: intercession from the intercessors qualified for it does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted, i.e., for his sake and concerning his matter, from among those deserving intercession on their behalf, not others who do not deserve it. The lam in "for whom" may be connected to the intercession itself.

Abu al-Baqa' said: as you say, "I interceded for him." It may also be connected to "benefit" (tanfaʿu), but the better view is that it is connected to the omitted element as we mentioned.

It has been said: What is meant by His saying, ﴿intercession does not benefit﴾ is that it does not exist at all except for one whom He has permitted. He attached the negation to its benefit rather than its occurrence, explicitly negating what was their purpose in its occurrence.

The majority read "adhina" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: Allah permitted him, since His name, glorified is He, is mentioned before this. Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, in the passive form, the one granting permission being Allah, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28].

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the fear of these intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, saying: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts﴾. The majority read "fuzzi'a" in the passive form, the agent being Allah, and the substitute for the agent being the prepositional phrase. Ibn ʿAmir read "fazza'a" in the active form, its subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He. Both readings have the doubled zay, and the form fa''ala (taf'īl) has the meaning of removal, so tafzīʿ is the removal of fear.

Al-Hasan read like the majority's reading, except that he lightened the zay.

Qutrub said: the meaning of ﴿removed from their hearts﴾ is: what was in them of terror, which is fear, was taken out.

Mujahid said: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning: intercession does not come from any of these worshipped ones other than Allah—from the angels, the prophets, or the idols—except that Allah, glorified is He, permits the angels, the prophets, and their like to intercede for whomever deserves it, and they are in the utmost fear of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they are in awe of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. When He permits them to intercede, they are struck with terror because of the tremendous matter that accompanies that state, and the intense fear lest something of Allah's decrees occur. When it is lifted from them, they say to the angels above them—and they are those who convey the revelation by permission—﴿What has your Lord said?﴾, meaning: what has He commanded? They say to them: He has said the truth, which is: accepting your intercession for those who deserve it, and not others. He is the Most High, the Great, so He may judge among His servants as He wills and do as He desires.

It has been said: this terror occurs to the angels at every command the Lord issues.

The meaning: intercession benefits only from the angels who, today, are in fear and obedient to Allah, not from inanimate things and devils.

It has also been said: those who say, "What has your Lord said?" are the ones being interceded for, and those who answer them are the intercessors from among the angels and prophets.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: until the terror is uncovered from the hearts of the polytheists in the Hereafter. The angels say to them: "What did your Lord say in the world?" They say: "The truth," and they confess at a time when confession will not benefit them.

Ibn ʿUmar and Qatadah read "farragha" with an unpointed ra and a pointed ghayn, from al-faraagh (emptiness). The meaning: Allah emptied their hearts, i.e., removed fear from them.

Ibn Mas'ud read "ifranqiʿa," with an unpointed ra after the fa', then a nun, then a qaf, then an unpointed ʿayn, from al-ifrinqiʿah, which means dispersal.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to rebuke and reprove the polytheists, saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: who bestows upon you these provisions from which you benefit? For your deities do not possess an atom's weight. Provision from the sky is rain and what is benefited from it, such as the sun, the moon and the stars; provision from the earth is plants, minerals and the like. Since the disbelievers were unable to answer this question, and their minds would not accept attributing this provision to their deities, and they might hesitate to attribute it to Allah for fear that the proof would be established against them, Allah commanded His Messenger to answer it, saying: ﴿Say: Allah﴾, i.e., it is He who provides for you from the heavens and the earth. Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to inform them that they are upon error—but in a fair manner regarding the argument, after the description of who is upon guidance and who is upon error had preceded. He said: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾. The meaning: one of the two groups—those who affirm Allah as the Creator and Provider and single Him out for worship, or those who worship inanimate things that cannot create, provide, benefit or harm—is indeed upon one of the two states, guidance or error. It is known to every intelligent person that whoever worships the One who creates, provides, benefits and harms is the one upon guidance, and whoever worships that which cannot create, provide, benefit or harm is the one upon error. Thus this statement has included the explanation of the party of guidance, who are the Muslims, and the party of error, who are the polytheists, in a manner more eloquent than explicit statement.

Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of this statement is the meaning of the words of one who is clear-sighted in argument to his companion: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he is the truthful, correct one and his companion the lying, mistaken one.

He said: "aw" (or), according to the Basrans, retains its own function and is not for doubt, but it is in the manner the Arabs use in such a context when the speaker does not wish to clarify while knowing the meaning.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it means "wa" (and), and its sense is: "Indeed we are upon guidance and you are in clear error," and from this is the verse of Jarir:

Do you think, Tha'labah of the horsemen, or Rabah, that they have equalled Tuhayyah and al-Rabab with them?

i.e., Tha'labah and Rabah. Likewise is the saying of another:

So when the severity of war intensified among us, we considered Rabah and Rizam.

i.e., and Rizam. His saying "aw iyyakum" is conjoined to the subject of "inna," and its predicate is the one mentioned; the predicate of the second is omitted for indication of it, i.e., "Indeed we are upon guidance or in clear error, and indeed you are upon guidance or in clear error." It is also permissible the reverse: that the mentioned one is the predicate of the second, and the predicate of the first is omitted, as already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

Then He, glorified is He, followed this fair statement with a statement more eloquent in fairness and further from disputation and contention, saying: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we have committed, and we will not be questioned about what you do﴾, meaning: I only call you to what is good for you and beneficial, and your disbelief and your abandonment of responding to me do not harm me. This is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6]. In attributing the crime to the Muslims and ascribing the general term "work" to the addressees, while the works of the Muslims are pure righteousness and pure obedience, and the works of the disbelievers are clear disobedience and manifest sin, there is a degree of fairness that cannot be measured.

The intended meaning is conciliation and mutual disengagement, and this verse and its like have been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to threaten them with the punishment of the Hereafter, but in a manner that is not explicit, saying: ﴿Say: Our Lord will bring us together﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿then He will judge between us with truth﴾, i.e., He will decide and judge between us with truth, rewarding the obedient and punishing the disobedient. He is al-Fattah, i.e., the Judge who rules by truth, who decides by what is right, the Knower of what pertains to His judgment and decree from among the interests.

This too has been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

The returning pronoun of the relative is omitted, i.e., "you have attached them." It is also permissible that it is the sight of the eye, the verb being transitive by the hamza to two: the first the ya', the second the relative pronoun, and "partners" being in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Then He refuted what they claim of partners and nullified that, saying: ﴿No! Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, i.e., refrain from the claim of partnership; rather, the One who is solely possessed of divinity is Allah, the Mighty by dominance and triumph, the Wise by His dazzling wisdom.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock, it penetrates them. When terror is removed from their hearts, they say, 'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'To the One who spoke the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" The hadith continues, and there are other hadiths with similar meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ that he said: "We are upon guidance, and you are in clear error."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "al-Fattah is the Judge."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 34, verses 22–27:

His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Allah﴾. This is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to say this statement to the disbelievers of Quraysh, or to the disbelievers in general. The two objects of "claim" (zaʿamtum) are omitted, meaning: "whom you claimed to be gods," the context indicating them.

Muqatil said: It means, "Call upon them so that they may remove from you the harm which has befallen you in the years of hunger."

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them, saying: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth﴾, meaning: they have no power over good or evil, nor over bringing benefit or repelling harm in any matter whatsoever. He mentioned the heavens and the earth to intend generality, since they are the container of the existing things. ﴿And they have no share therein﴾, meaning: the deities have no partnership in the heavens and the earth, neither in creation, nor in ownership, nor in disposal. ﴿And for Him there is not among them any supporter﴾, meaning: for Allah, glorified is He, there is none among those deities who assists Him in any matter of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.

﴿And intercession with Him does not benefit﴾, meaning: the intercession of those who intercede with Him from among the angels and others. His saying: ﴿except for one whom He has permitted﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general circumstances, meaning: intercession does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for, from among the angels, the prophets, and their like from the people of knowledge and action. It is known that these do not intercede except for one who deserves intercession, not for the disbelievers. It is also possible that the meaning is: intercession from the intercessors qualified for it does not benefit in any circumstance except when it is for one whom He has permitted, i.e., for his sake and concerning his matter, from among those deserving intercession on their behalf, not others who do not deserve it. The lam in "for whom" may be connected to the intercession itself.

Abu al-Baqa' said: as you say, "I interceded for him." It may also be connected to "benefit" (tanfaʿu), but the better view is that it is connected to the omitted element as we mentioned.

It has been said: What is meant by His saying, ﴿intercession does not benefit﴾ is that it does not exist at all except for one whom He has permitted. He attached the negation to its benefit rather than its occurrence, explicitly negating what was their purpose in its occurrence.

The majority read "adhina" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: Allah permitted him, since His name, glorified is He, is mentioned before this. Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, in the passive form, the one granting permission being Allah, glorified is He. A similar verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28].

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the fear of these intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, saying: ﴿until, when terror is removed from their hearts﴾. The majority read "fuzzi'a" in the passive form, the agent being Allah, and the substitute for the agent being the prepositional phrase. Ibn ʿAmir read "fazza'a" in the active form, its subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He. Both readings have the doubled zay, and the form fa''ala (taf'īl) has the meaning of removal, so tafzīʿ is the removal of fear.

Al-Hasan read like the majority's reading, except that he lightened the zay.

Qutrub said: the meaning of ﴿removed from their hearts﴾ is: what was in them of terror, which is fear, was taken out.

Mujahid said: the veil is uncovered from their hearts on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning: intercession does not come from any of these worshipped ones other than Allah—from the angels, the prophets, or the idols—except that Allah, glorified is He, permits the angels, the prophets, and their like to intercede for whomever deserves it, and they are in the utmost fear of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they are in awe of Him﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. When He permits them to intercede, they are struck with terror because of the tremendous matter that accompanies that state, and the intense fear lest something of Allah's decrees occur. When it is lifted from them, they say to the angels above them—and they are those who convey the revelation by permission—﴿What has your Lord said?﴾, meaning: what has He commanded? They say to them: He has said the truth, which is: accepting your intercession for those who deserve it, and not others. He is the Most High, the Great, so He may judge among His servants as He wills and do as He desires.

It has been said: this terror occurs to the angels at every command the Lord issues.

The meaning: intercession benefits only from the angels who, today, are in fear and obedient to Allah, not from inanimate things and devils.

It has also been said: those who say, "What has your Lord said?" are the ones being interceded for, and those who answer them are the intercessors from among the angels and prophets.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: until the terror is uncovered from the hearts of the polytheists in the Hereafter. The angels say to them: "What did your Lord say in the world?" They say: "The truth," and they confess at a time when confession will not benefit them.

Ibn ʿUmar and Qatadah read "farragha" with an unpointed ra and a pointed ghayn, from al-faraagh (emptiness). The meaning: Allah emptied their hearts, i.e., removed fear from them.

Ibn Mas'ud read "ifranqiʿa," with an unpointed ra after the fa', then a nun, then a qaf, then an unpointed ʿayn, from al-ifrinqiʿah, which means dispersal.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to rebuke and reprove the polytheists, saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?﴾, meaning: who bestows upon you these provisions from which you benefit? For your deities do not possess an atom's weight. Provision from the sky is rain and what is benefited from it, such as the sun, the moon and the stars; provision from the earth is plants, minerals and the like. Since the disbelievers were unable to answer this question, and their minds would not accept attributing this provision to their deities, and they might hesitate to attribute it to Allah for fear that the proof would be established against them, Allah commanded His Messenger to answer it, saying: ﴿Say: Allah﴾, i.e., it is He who provides for you from the heavens and the earth. Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to inform them that they are upon error—but in a fair manner regarding the argument, after the description of who is upon guidance and who is upon error had preceded. He said: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾. The meaning: one of the two groups—those who affirm Allah as the Creator and Provider and single Him out for worship, or those who worship inanimate things that cannot create, provide, benefit or harm—is indeed upon one of the two states, guidance or error. It is known to every intelligent person that whoever worships the One who creates, provides, benefits and harms is the one upon guidance, and whoever worships that which cannot create, provide, benefit or harm is the one upon error. Thus this statement has included the explanation of the party of guidance, who are the Muslims, and the party of error, who are the polytheists, in a manner more eloquent than explicit statement.

Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning of this statement is the meaning of the words of one who is clear-sighted in argument to his companion: "One of us is a liar," while he knows that he is the truthful, correct one and his companion the lying, mistaken one.

He said: "aw" (or), according to the Basrans, retains its own function and is not for doubt, but it is in the manner the Arabs use in such a context when the speaker does not wish to clarify while knowing the meaning.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it means "wa" (and), and its sense is: "Indeed we are upon guidance and you are in clear error," and from this is the verse of Jarir:

Do you think, Tha'labah of the horsemen, or Rabah, that they have equalled Tuhayyah and al-Rabab with them?

i.e., Tha'labah and Rabah. Likewise is the saying of another:

So when the severity of war intensified among us, we considered Rabah and Rizam.

i.e., and Rizam. His saying "aw iyyakum" is conjoined to the subject of "inna," and its predicate is the one mentioned; the predicate of the second is omitted for indication of it, i.e., "Indeed we are upon guidance or in clear error, and indeed you are upon guidance or in clear error." It is also permissible the reverse: that the mentioned one is the predicate of the second, and the predicate of the first is omitted, as already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

Then He, glorified is He, followed this fair statement with a statement more eloquent in fairness and further from disputation and contention, saying: ﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we have committed, and we will not be questioned about what you do﴾, meaning: I only call you to what is good for you and beneficial, and your disbelief and your abandonment of responding to me do not harm me. This is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6]. In attributing the crime to the Muslims and ascribing the general term "work" to the addressees, while the works of the Muslims are pure righteousness and pure obedience, and the works of the disbelievers are clear disobedience and manifest sin, there is a degree of fairness that cannot be measured.

The intended meaning is conciliation and mutual disengagement, and this verse and its like have been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to threaten them with the punishment of the Hereafter, but in a manner that is not explicit, saying: ﴿Say: Our Lord will bring us together﴾, i.e., on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿then He will judge between us with truth﴾, i.e., He will decide and judge between us with truth, rewarding the obedient and punishing the disobedient. He is al-Fattah, i.e., the Judge who rules by truth, who decides by what is right, the Knower of what pertains to His judgment and decree from among the interests.

This too has been abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to present to them another argument by which he shows what they are upon of error, saying: ﴿Say: Show me those whom you have attached to Him as partners﴾, i.e., show me those whom you have attached to Allah as partners to Him. This seeing is the heart-seeing, so "partners" is the third object, since the verb is transitive by the hamza to three: the first being the ya' in "arawni," the second the relative pronoun, and the third "partners." The returning pronoun of the relative is omitted, i.e., "you have attached them." It is also permissible that it is the sight of the eye, the verb being transitive by the hamza to two: the first the ya', the second the relative pronoun, and "partners" being in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Then He refuted what they claim of partners and nullified that, saying: ﴿No! Rather, He is Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, i.e., refrain from the claim of partnership; rather, the One who is solely possessed of divinity is Allah, the Mighty by dominance and triumph, the Wise by His dazzling wisdom.

(p-1198) Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿until terror is removed from their hearts﴾ that he said: "It is made manifest."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him that he said: "When the Compeller revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), He called the Messenger from among the angels to convey the revelation. The angels heard the voice of the Compeller speaking the revelation, and when it was lifted from their hearts they asked him what Allah had said, and they said, 'The truth,' and they knew that Allah does not say anything but the truth."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The sound of the revelation was like the sound of iron on rock. When they heard it they fell down in prostration, and when they raised their heads they said, ﴿What has your Lord said? They say: The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.﴾

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also that he said: "The command descends to the lowest heaven with a sound like the sound of a chain on a stone. All the inhabitants of the heavens are struck with terror by it and say, 'What has your Lord said?' Then they return to themselves and say, 'The truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'"

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah decrees a matter in the heaven, the angels strike their wings in submission to His word, like a chain upon smooth rock, it penetrates them. When terror is removed from their hearts, they say, 'What has your Lord said?' They say, 'To the One who spoke the truth, and He is the Most High, the Great.'" The hadith continues, and there are other hadiths with similar meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿIkrimah regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ that he said: "We are upon guidance, and you are in clear error."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "al-Fattah is the Judge."

In the placement of kāffatan there are several views. It is said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the kāf in arsalnāka. Al-Zajjāj said: meaning, "We did not send you except as one who gathers people together in warning and conveying (the message)." Kāffah here means "the one who gathers," and the hāʾ in it is for emphasis, like ʿallāmah.

Abū Ḥayyān said: As for al-Zajjāj's statement that kāffatan means "gathering" and the hāʾ is for emphasis, the language does not support it, because kaffa does not mean "gather"; rather it means "prevent." One says kaffa yakuffu, meaning "he prevented, he restrains."

The meaning is: "except as one who restrains them from disbelief." From this comes al-kaff (the hand), because it restrains what is in it from coming out.

It is also said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with the hāʾ for emphasis, like al-ʿāqibah and al-ʿāfiyah, and the intended meaning is that it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "except as a comprehensive message."

It is also said that it is a circumstantial of "the people," and the construction is: "We did not send you except to the people, all of them." This was rejected on the grounds that a circumstantial may not precede its governing word when that word is in the genitive, as is established in the science of i'rāb (grammatical analysis).

This objection may be answered by saying that Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, Ibn Kaysān and Ibn Burhān permitted this, and from it is the poet's verse:

*When the man is weary of leadership while still young, its pursuit is hard for him when he is grown.*

And the verse of another:

*I consoled myself for you, all of you, after our parting, with remembering you, until you seemed to me present.*

And the verse of another:

*Heedless, death confronts the man, and he is called, but there is no time for refusal.*

Among those who preferred that it be a circumstantial of the genitive that follows it is Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, who said: it was placed first for emphasis and reinforcement.

It is also said that the meaning is "except one possessing comprehensiveness," i.e., possessing restraint, so the modified noun is omitted.

It is said that the lām in lil-nās carries the sense of ilā ("to"), i.e., "We did not send you to the people except as one who gathers them together through warning and conveying, or restrains them from disbelief and sins." The accusative of bashīran and nadhīran is a circumstantial: "bringing them good news of Paradise, and warning them of the Fire." But most people do not know what is with Allah of benefit in the sending of messengers.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ That is: when will this promise come about, the one you make to us, which is the establishment of the Hour? Inform us of it if you are truthful. They said this in a manner of mockery toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those believers with him. So Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer on their behalf, and he said: ﴿Say: "For you is an appointed time of a day"﴾ That is: a set time of a day, namely the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: the time of the arrival of death. It is also said: he meant the Day of Badr, because it was a day of their punishment in this world. In any case, this idāfah (construction) is explanatory. Regarding mīʿād, it may be a verbal noun meaning "the promise," or it may be a noun of time.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-waʿd, al-waʿīd and al-mīʿād have the same meaning.

Ibn Abī ʿAblah read mīʿādun with tanwīn and nominative case, and yawman in the accusative, taking mīʿādun as a subject, yawman as an adverbial, and the predicate as lakum.

ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read mīʿādu nominative with tanwīn, and yawmi in the genitive, being idāfah to the clause following it.

The grammarians permitted "mīʿādun yawmun," with both nominative and tanwīn, taking mīʿādun as the subject and yawmun as an apposition to it. The clause "you will not delay from it an hour, nor advance" is an attribute of mīʿād, meaning: this appointed promise made for you, you cannot delay from it nor advance beyond it, but it will certainly occur at the time Allah has decreed for its occurrence.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned a portion of the ugly deeds of the disbelievers and a type of their disbelief, and said: ﴿And those who disbelieved say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an nor in that which is before it"﴾, meaning the earlier scriptures, such as the Torah and the Gospel, and the earlier messengers.

It is also said that what is meant by "that which is before it" is the Hereafter.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of their condition in the Hereafter, and said: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), or to everyone suitable for it. The meaning of "made to stand before their Lord" is: they are held back at the place of reckoning, (p-1199) ﴿returning speech to one another﴾, i.e., they exchange accusations among themselves with blame and reproach, after having been, in the world, opposed and supportive and loving of one another.

Then He, glorified is He, explained that exchange, and said: ﴿Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant (i.e., the leaders who were followed)﴾: "Had you not turned us away from faith in Allah and from following His Messenger, we would have been believers in Allah, affirming His Messenger and his Book." ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were deemed weak﴾, responding to them and rejecting what they said: ﴿Did we turn you away from the guidance﴾, i.e., did we prevent you from faith after the guidance had come to you? They said this denying what they were accused of, and disowning what they were charged with regarding turning them away. Then they explained to them that it was they themselves who turned away from themselves, who refused guidance after it had come to them, so they said: ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾, i.e., persistent in disbelief, greatly sinful, and great in wrongdoing.

﴿And those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, in reply to what they had answered them, and in rejection of what they had charged them with regarding their own turning away: ﴿Rather, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾. The root of makr in Arabic speech is deception and stratagem; one says makara bihi when he deceives him and plots against him.

The meaning is: "Rather, your scheming against us by night and by day," so the genitive complement was omitted, and the adverb was put in its place for breadth of expression.

Al-Akhfash said: it is on the estimate "this is the scheming of the night and the day."

Al-Naḥḥās said: the meaning, and Allah knows best, is "Rather, your scheming in the night and the day, and your calling us to disbelief, is what led us to this."

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: "Rather, your deeds by night and by day." It is permissible to make the night and the day the ones who scheme, by metaphorical attribution, as is established in the science of ma'ānī.

Al-Mubarrad said: as the Arabs say, "its day is fasting and its night is standing," and he recited the verse of Jarīr:

*You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylān, on the night journey, and you slept, while the night of the camels is not sleeping.*

And Sībawayh recited:

*Standing through my night and the unveiling of my worry.*

Qatādah and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read makrun in the nominative with tanwīn, and al-layla and al-nahāra in the accusative, the estimate being: "Rather, there is a scheming occurring in the night and the day."

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Abū Razīn read with fatḥah on the kāf and shaddah on the rāʾ, in idāfah, with the meaning of "turning around," from karra yakurru, when it comes and goes. The nominative of makru in these readings is either as a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "the scheming of the night and the day turned us away," or as the subject of an omitted verb, i.e., "the scheming of the night and the day turned us away," or as the predicate of an omitted subject, as mentioned earlier from al-Akhfash.

Ṭalḥah ibn Rāshid read as Saʿīd ibn Jubayr did, but he put makru in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., "Rather, you repeat the seduction as a constant scheme, never ceasing from it." The accusative of idh tamurūnanā is that it is an adverb of the scheming: "Rather, your scheming against us was at the time you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and to make for Him rivals (andād), i.e., likenesses and equals."

Al-Mubarrad said: one says, "the nidd of so-and-so is so-and-so," meaning his equal, and he recited:

*Do you Taym make for me a rival, when Taym is not of noble lineage with an equal?*

The pronoun in His words ﴿And they concealed the regret when they saw the punishment﴾ refers to both groups, i.e., both groups concealed the regret over what they had done of disbelief, and hid it from others, or each of them concealed it from the other, fearing mockery.

It is also said that what is meant by asarrū here is "they displayed," since it is one of the words with opposite meanings: it is sometimes used in the sense of concealment and sometimes in the sense of disclosure, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*I passed through guards and terrors of a people who watched me, though they would have revealed my killing.*

It is also said that the meaning of asarrū here is: the regret became visible in the furrows of their faces.

﴿And We placed the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. Al-aghlāl is the plural of ghull; one says, "on his neck is a ghull of iron," meaning iron shackles were placed on the necks of these people in the Fire. What is meant by "those who disbelieved" is those previously mentioned, and the explicit mention is for added condemnation, or it refers to disbelievers in general, so these people enter it in a primary sense. ﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾, i.e., except the recompense of what they used to do of association with Allah, or "except for what they used to do," with the preposition omitted.

Ibn Abī Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujāhid, regarding His words ﴿And We did not send you except comprehensively to mankind﴾, that he said: "to the people, all of them."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah, who said: Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to the Arabs and the non-Arabs, and the most honored of them before Allah are the most obedient to Him.

These same narrators also narrated from him regarding His words ﴿And those who disbelieved say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an"﴾, that he said: this is the saying of the polytheists of the Arabs, who disbelieved in the Qur'an and in that which is before it of the books and prophets.

*When the man is weary of leadership while still young, its pursuit is hard for him when he is grown.*

And the verse of another:

*I consoled myself for you, all of you, after our parting, with remembering you, until you seemed to me present.*

And the verse of another:

*Heedless, death confronts the man, and he is called, but there is no time for refusal.*

Among those who preferred that it be a circumstantial of the genitive that follows it is Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, who said: it was placed first for emphasis and reinforcement.

It is also said that the meaning is "except one possessing comprehensiveness," i.e., possessing restraint, so the modified noun is omitted.

But most people do not know what is with Allah of benefit in the sending of messengers.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ That is: when will this promise come about, the one you make to us, which is the establishment of the Hour? Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-waʿd, al-waʿīd and al-mīʿād have the same meaning.

Then He, glorified is He, informed of their condition in the Hereafter, and said: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Then He, glorified is He, explained that exchange, and said: ﴿Those who were deemed weak will say to those who were arrogant (i.e., the leaders who were followed)﴾: "Had you not turned us away from faith in Allah and from following His Messenger, we would have been believers in Allah, affirming His Messenger and his Book." ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were deemed weak﴾, responding to them and rejecting what they said: ﴿Did we turn you away from the guidance﴾, i.e., did we prevent you from faith after the guidance had come to you? Then they explained to them that it was they themselves who turned away from themselves, who refused guidance after it had come to them, so they said: ﴿Rather, you were criminals﴾, i.e., persistent in disbelief, greatly sinful, and great in wrongdoing.
